utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances now?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor of law from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, along with my colleague, Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic, along with Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston, Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear here on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo, along with my co-counsel, Ms. Cynthia McMurrey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, what is the position now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Landzo is here and we are ready to provided, of course. I think -- my understanding is that the Registry was preparing a memo about what happened that was supposed to be circulated to us all yesterday. I have not got it yet, maybe some of you have. That is all I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually we had to adjourn at your insistence because your client was not here and so we try to find out what happened. That is why I asked you what the position is, in case you might be able to help. I am satisfied he is here so we can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He is here and we are ready to proceed, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may continue with my submission in relation to documents that were seized by the Austrian authorities, your Honours, having regard to the time that has been lost this week and the need to move ahead with this, unless your Honours have any views as to the contrary, I think it may be more efficient if I proceed to deal with it as one submission, rather than breaking it at the end of each document. That would then enable counsel for the Defence to then respond by way of one submission, which I think may expedite the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually I have always thought from the beginning, if you are depending on the established indicia of admissibility, nothing stops you making a submission and then relating the documents you rely for such satisfaction of indicia and that should be sufficient and then the Defence can reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I will endeavour to proceed through the matter as quickly as possible. I think it is also necessary for me to make submissions as to relevance too at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is satisfying admissibility. You have to show how these documents, whether taken together or individually, have satisfied these indicia of admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next document, Exhibit 126, might that be displayed on the screen, please? This document, your Honours, is a hand-written document, written in Bosnian, and signed at the end with the name "flame" or "oganj", which I have previously referred to in my submissions. It is a document in hand-written form addressed to the main staff of the supreme command of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is directed to be submitted to the chief of the main staff, and bears the date 27th April 1993. When shown this document, Mr. Moerbauer, in his evidence at page 3653, lines 14 to 16, said of the document: "The document was also in binder I5 and was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at police headquarters in Vienna following the search." Your Honours, the structure of the document is in the nature of a report. Those matters, which we say go to the reliability of the document in terms of how they fit with other pieces of evidence that your Honours have heard, include what is referred to in the first paragraph at the top of the page of that document, where the second sentence starts: "Due to the fact that I knew them personally and the fact that the Croatian media wrote and reported that I had gone over to the Chetniks." Your Honours may recall in document 124, Exhibit 124, the reference to this question of going over to the Chetniks or the Croatian media was also referred to in that document. Perhaps if we could quickly just go to that document, 124, the second page , and in the centre of that page under paragraph 3 there it is, the paragraph that commences: "According to some Croatian newspapers, I had flown in a helicopter", et cetera, et cetera. Your Honours, now if we may go back, please, again to document 126, the first page, there is a reference there, your Honours, in paragraph 1, the first sentence: "During the conflict between the HVO and the army in Konjic, about 300 fully armed HVO members sided with the Chetniks in Borci." Your Honours, in our submission this is a reference to the well known dispute that had developed between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the course of 1992, which escalated to the point that there was in fact open conflict in the very latter part of 1992, continuing on through 1993. Your Honours, if we may go to document 130, on page 4 of that document, down the bottom of the page, starting with the paragraph (f), in this document, your Honours, which I will come to in due course, and it is a document which we say was written by the accused Mucic about Delalic, but I will deal with that later, paragraph (f) says: "Delalic insisted that we attack Borci a week after Bradina and that the entire municipality be cleansed. However, that could not be done because the HVO withdrew immediately after Bradina, unwilling to take part in that operation. This is when the first fierce clash between Konjic HVO, Konjic TO, with Zejnil in the focus of attention." In my submission, your Honour, it picks up that theme of the difficulties that existed between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially in relation to Konjic. Going back now to Exhibit 126, again on the first page, there is a reference then to events which are referred to especially in connection with the Neretva valley. The reference in paragraph 2: "The Konjic army command believes that only one HVO company from the villages of Turija and Bijela crossed over to the Chetnik sides, because they were no longer there. Nevertheless at night the main HVO forces crossed the lake by boat from right side of the Neretva and together with Croatian and Serbian inhabitants went via Celebici and dug in artillery", et cetera. Your Honours, in Exhibit 129, there is a reference, your Honours, to this incident -- I am having difficulty locating it just at the moment. Perhaps I might come back to that. I will just go on. Dealing with again this Exhibit 126, if we can go through to the third page of that document, there is a reference there to the need to announce in all media that Konjic and Jablanica, about 300 HVO officers had joined units in Borci and the necessity for that to be made public. That, your Honours, the fact that these things were made public on a previous occasion, is also referred to in communications -- in these documents, particularly starting with Exhibit 129 at page 15, at the very top of the page . There is a reference there to an alleged agreement existing between the Croats and the Serbs in relation to the Neretva valley river, and the parts of it where they would agree to occupy. At the top of the page it says: "On the basis of intelligence and operational checks, it has been discovered that since the beginning of the war the HVO has been permanently working on the creation of its own HZ-HB state, to which the borders have already been decided. The border of Bradina on the right bank of the Neretva river, which has been decided at a meeting between Milosevic and Tudjman." Then, your Honours, going back to Exhibit 126 at that point that we were before, if we may, on page 3, there is in that paragraph, it is a long sentence, but starting: "The overall intention and plan mentioned that the rumours which spread a long time ago about the deal between Boban and Karadzic" -- your Honours may know also represent the interests of the Croats and Serbs respectively, but in this instance, the Croats and Serbs of Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather than of Serbia and Croatia, on the partition of Herzegovina along the Neretva river is to materialise and so forth. So again, your Honours, we submit this is just one small reference to the issue, but again an important one. In terms of the relevance of the document, your Honours, it is more a document that goes to lend support to other documents by references in it, so it can be shown that the concepts and issues that have been stated have been repeated in other documents, lending, in our submission, to the argument of its consistency and therefore reliability, but the document does have relevance additional to that as well. Your Honours, on page 5, and if we could go to the top of page 5 of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, remember when you started I wanted to find out actually what these documents are intended to be tendered for. Can you kindly remind us what the real purpose of tendering all these documents is, so that we will know exactly how, even if remotely, you concern some of these documents, because if you consider that anywhere where reference has been made to these conflicts might be referred to as relevant to the issue, you should let us know exactly what it is tendered for.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, this particular document that I am dealing with has a twofold purpose. One is that it contains within it material which we say is of itself directly relevant, but I was just stating that it goes more to being part of the pattern of evidence. In our submission, a document found on the premises, which goes to a pattern and fits in with other documents, has a relevance on that basis, because it lends support to establishing the authenticity and reliability of other documents which perhaps are of greater relevance and importance to the proceedings. But this document itself has its own, in our submission, relevance, and I will go to that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Perhaps I have not made myself understood. What is the purpose of tendering them? There must be a reason, either to identify particular persons for what they have done in relation to the Trial or their indictment before the Trial Chamber. We have heard they are all participating in the war effort. You now tender them for particular purposes. These are the purposes one would like to understand, so that we can see their relevance to those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought I explained that, your Honour, but I will explain it again. That has a twofold purpose. Perhaps I will explain the second purpose before the first one, which may make it perhaps a little easier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not only this document, the series of documents, so if we know why they are being tendered, and you formulate the reason why they are being tendered, they are tendered to show 1, 2, 3, something like that, then we will know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, overall, as a general proposition, they go to establish the command responsibility of the accused Delalic; to a lesser extent the responsibilities of the accused Mucic, and in particular with reference to the Celebici camp. But this is a complex issue, it is not something that can be -- I cannot simply give you one document or produce one witness that can do that. It is a complex and difficult process, but it is a combination of documents which we submit at the end of the day go to establish that point and clearly do, but cannot be done in isolation. It has to be considered in combination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I seem to agree with you, not being a party to the dispute myself, it should be clearly brought out what you are pursuing. If it is command responsibility, the command structure and the way each one fits into any particular pattern, I think that is your responsibility, and the relevance of the documents to such a proposition, this is what perhaps I would like to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I add, you have led evidence to show that he was a co-ordinator to begin with, then commander of Tactical Group 1. He was interested in military affairs. All these documents merely show his interest in defending his country, nothing more than that. How does it really fit in with this commander structure, as my learned brother has pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With respect, your Honour, I think they go further than that. If I may, I would like to demonstrate how much further they go than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I appreciate that. I know you are still continuing, you may still conclude, but by the time you have, the picture might be obvious where this command structure lies, which therefore indicates his responsibility for what he has been accused of. This is what I thought you were pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Your Honours, to deal with that issue straight away, one of the questions is the connection between the accused Delalic and the prisoners themselves, and the military significance, or an explanation of the military significance, of why it is that prisoners would be taken and placed in Celebici, and if they were taken and placed in Celebici camp, for what purpose that was done, and if it is in relation to the military strategy of the accused Delalic this would do that, and in our submission that is one indicia of his responsibility towards those people that are placed in the camp. So if the Prosecution can show that even though he was not there at the camp on a day-to-day basis, part of his role was to -- was, as leading the military, the battle, so to speak, was taking prisoners, and then he was directly responsible for having those prisoners interned in the camp, then there is a command responsibility to those people who he interns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In fact this is one of the problems I have too. I do not remember every hearing anybody, including the prisoners, as being under Tactical Group 1 of which he is commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They were captured by that Group, is that what your Honour is saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, not captured by them. The group was formed on 11th July. He took over as commander of the Tactical Group on 11th July. I do not think any prisoners entered that camp after 11th July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours, and certainly it will be the method of military operation which we again say would be illustrated by these documents that would go to that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: These documents you are producing show he is interested in affairs, he knows what is happening, nothing more than that. They do not establish command responsibility, these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With respect, your Honour, I do believe they do go further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is why I normally give you a free hand to put forward these arguments, and finally we look into it and see whether they meet the requirements of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have two obligations. Relevance is one thing. I could go through and make my submissions on relevance and then be confronted with the submission from the Defence, "They are not reliable, you cannot rely on them even if they are relevant", so I do have the dual responsibility to meet; other than we break up the submission into two parts, which I do not mind doing, establishing relevance first and then coming back and dealing with reliability and whether or not they should be admitted. But the process of establishing the authenticity and reliability is a complex and difficult process, an intricate process. I am happy to do it that way, if your Honours would just wish me to deal with relevance, I am happy to do that. If you wish me to go through and deal with relevance, I am happy to do that and come back and meet the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We have heard your arguments that these are related to the whole exercise; all stories related to the exercise of the war effort and the participation of Delalic, Mucic, all of them, and reports by other members of the same outfit as to what happened, which involves Delalic, Mucic and all of them. I suppose one can say intrinsically that can be relevant, but that does not help one if you are looking for the real responsibility for the area in which they are charged, which is a different consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, one of the issues that I say this document goes to is why were the prisoners captured? Why were they put in the camp? The answer to that is: they wanted to use them for exchange. They wanted to do two things: they wanted to reduce the number of available manpower to the opposing forces, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, but who wanted to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the second reason was they wanted to use them for the purposes of exchange, so they could get back their own men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who wanted to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Inferences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The world is made of inferences, your Honour. In my submission, this document does show that there is a pattern of approach, a pattern of approach which was still valid and consistent in 1993 when this report was written, we say, by the accused Delalic using his code name, and the document that is presently shown on the screen, at the top of the page, in our submission goes to that. It is a reference to future operation, but nevertheless the military procedure is consistent with what happened in 1992, where it says: "Here it is necessary to completely crush the HVO forces, capture their ammunition and all their members for exchange."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course. I am saying this is -- why should the processes be any different when dealing with a military action against the HVO than if you are dealing with a military action against the Chetniks? In my submission, your Honours, there is consistence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is speaking of the perfidy of the HVO in this letter, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, but in my submission, your Honours, it is illustrative of a person who has a particular approach to military activity, and one which there is evidence of in 1992; namely the capturing of ammunition and members of the opposition, and then ultimately using them for the purposes of exchange, and that is set out in this document that is on your screen now. There is, your Honours, finally, a reference at the bottom to firstly, this is going over the final page, and if we may go to the final page, at the bottom of the page, a reference there to firstly: "Many regards to everybody, especially to Divjak", and your Honours have heard that Divjak was there during the period 1992, there with the accused Delalic, and again it is signed with this code name, "oganj", or "flame". Just in relation to that, the video Exhibit 116, there is an excerpt of that video in the transcript of the video at a particular scene in Borci on 28th June 1992, and there is a very small segment and it shows the accused Delalic making a radio telephone communication, and it shows the accused there and one can hear the telephone conversation from the accused's end, and it says: "002, do you hear me? Oganj calling." Then there is a voice from the other end and Delalic says: "Okay, Bijela coast, let us go." There is again conversation coming back from the other side and then he said -- the accused says: "002 switch off, Dido, do you hear Oganj 1 calling?" In my submission, that is in itself direct evidence that this is a term that was used by the accused in relation to, as it were, a military code name. Your Honours also saw it in Exhibit 124 at the final, last page of Exhibit 124 on the signature page, which is page 3, and perhaps just to refresh your Honours' minds again, the very bottom of the page we can see: "Greetings to the homeland, Oganj", and signed by Zejnil Delalic. So those, your Honours, are my submissions in relation to that particular document. We can now go to the next document, document 127. Could that be displayed on the screen, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I comment on this document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic's Defence is opposed to the admission of the document number 126 for the reasons mentioned before, because the Prosecution has not proved the authenticity or the relevance of the document they have tendered. I am not going to belabour the arguments that have already been mentioned regarding the reliability of this document, I am just going to repeat what I have stated before to this Trial Chamber. When this document is shown, I would like to request that it is shown in the original, so that we see the handwriting. We do not know when and by whom this document was compiled. We just see an English translation, which may leave a certain impression. I think that it will not leave the impression with the Trial Chamber, but it could somewhere, and this would be a distorted picture of what the document is. This document was hand-written, it is a document that allegedly was written in late April 1993, which is outside of the time-frame in the indictment. This is a document that allegedly, the way the Prosecution showed it, may have been drafted in Czechoslovakia. This is a document that never mentions Mr. Zejnil Delalic. This is a document that never mentions any command responsibility of anyone, including Mr. Delalic. It is talking about a time and relationship which have nothing to do with the subject of this indictment. Therefore, the reliability of this document is equally zero and the Prosecution is resorting to the same method; they are comparing other documents with this document, which has not been authenticated or shown to be relevant, and weaving a story about Mr. Delalic and his alleged command responsibility, which is contrary to anything that has been shown before this Trial Chamber. Therefore, your Honours, with respect to this document, the Prosecution points to the signature of "Oganj", which is supposedly a military code, and relates it to document 124. If this is a military code, as in document 124, that is already a method, secretive method, and they will not resort to it again in order to reveal their true name. We had expert testimonies by the Generals and the Trial Chamber has found out a number of facts regarding the Boracko Jezero military operations and they have nothing to do with the alleged proof that is offered through the documents here. So to repeat, this document has nothing to do with 1992, with the prison in Celebici, with the prisoners in the prison Celebici with Zejnil Delalic or with his command responsibility, so one more time, I plead with you, your Honours, given the absolutely unreliability of this document, we do not know who wrote it, I would like to take note of Rule 95, which speaks of the unreliability and if there is any doubt, as there is doubt in this, in the veracity of this document, I move to not accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I just, before you respond to that -- I had suggested that the more efficient way to deal with this would be for me to make one submission and then for counsel to then respond in a global fashion in the way that I would make my submission. I suggested that, your Honours, because I believed that it would be more efficient. The reason why I submit it is more efficient is that most of the submissions made in relation to individual documents are mere repetition of what has been said before. If your Honours wish to proceed that way, that is fine by me, but it will make the proceedings much more laborious and much lengthier when the general submission that can be made about failure to prove who wrote it, or whatever, is something that could be said presumably in relation to a number of them, and those -- it seems to me that this is a mere waste of time to have to deal with them document by document. I would urge your Honours to permit me to deal with it as one submission and then hear counsel, but if counsel -- if we are going to deal with it on a document by document basis, I have to indicate that it will take much longer than today and tomorrow and we will presumably have to adjourn it over until the next sittings to complete the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. Actually this was my error, because when you made that request, I agreed, I consented that perhaps the better thing was to make the submissions for admission of all the documents as a whole, and then the Defence can then reply, taking each of them the way they consider them inadmissible. I think that is the shorter method, and seeing them as a whole makes things easier for both the Prosecution and the Defence and I hope we will keep to that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now moving on, your Honour, to document 127, this document, your Honours, is a document which is in typewritten form. It bears a seal at the bottom of the document, and it also is a document that is stated or says to be signed by the co-ordinator, Zejnil Delalic, and then signed for the commander of the TO, Omer Boric and for the HVO commander, Dinko Zebic. Your Honours, the relevance of this document so far as the Prosecution is concerned are these: it is a document which expresses itself as an order. It is dated in Konjic, 3rd June 1992, and it relates to an order to open the railway to railway traffic from Jablanica, Konjic and Pazaric. We say it is relevant, your Honours, because it expressly deals with the area of operation the accused Delalic was involved in, but it also goes to the question of the accused's participation in the command process, as such. At this very early stage, 3rd June, there are three people involved in the issue of this command. It also, in our submission, is relevant because it goes to the broader question of the accused's authority to participate in this command process. Your Honours had seen in document 124, and I do not need to take your Honours to that, but document 124, this area, Jablanica, Konjic and Pazaric, is an area which the accused was involved in the Konjic area in terms of his areas of responsibility, even at that early stage. In the video, Exhibit 116, which I will take your Honours to subsequently, there is also, your Honours, a reference to this. There is a scene with an interviewer and Mr. Delalic, and the interviewer asks the question at the 0.42.02 minutes on the video, the interviewer asks the question: "Although you are not with us on the train, were you excited while you were waiting for it to arrive here in Jablanica." Zejnil Delalic answers: "Of course. As one of the organisers of this project, I can say I am very satisfied. Especially I have to give credit to the people working on the railway, who have taken this task very seriously. They have done everything, although the conditions were very difficult, everything was done on time, even better than in peacetime." Those are the words of the accused himself and in our submission directly relate to this particular order. Your Honours, in Exhibit 130, on page 4 of that exhibit, if we may just quickly go to that, down the bottom there is a paragraph (e) and if that could be enlarged. In this it says: "Five days later and quite on his own, he organised the first rail transport along the Jablanica, Konjic, Pazaric line with free tickets for everybody." In our submission, this is a document that was written by the accused Mucic and in our submission relates to this particular exhibit. We submit it is relevant and admissible on that basis. Moving to the next document, your Honours, Exhibit 128, if that could please be displayed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make a specific objection with regard to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose we would like to keep to the procedure we would like to adopt. It has not been admitted. All the admission will be determined after you have made your own contribution. We note your objection, that you object to all that has been tendered, so when you make your contribution you can raise all the points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document, document 128, is again one of the documents that form part of the military prosecutor's documents that were referred to -- was referred to particularly by General Pasalic in his evidence, and indeed go to some of the specific documents that were looked at and indeed admitted and accepted into evidence through the witness Pasalic. Again, your Honours, the only aspect of this document for which we say it is relevant is the reference to the accused Delalic and Mucic in particular, and in particular, reference to their positions. Firstly, in the centre of the page, we say it is relevant that there is a reference there in the paragraph numbered 1 to the fact that Zejnil Delalic is described by the military commander -- sorry, the military prosecutor as: "A serviceman commander of the first Tactical Group based in Konjic." Then there is a reference to the second defendant, Zdravko Mucic: "Serviceman commander of the military prison in Celebici." This document also makes reference to other accused before the court. There is a reference three lines from the very bottom of that page to the deputy, Hazim Delic, and also there is a reference further on to a prison guard, there is a reference to Osman Dedic and then Esad Landzo. I know that the spelling of Landzo in at least my copy of the translation appears to be wrong. Whether in the original it is spelt wrong, I cannot say, but I know over the page in relation to that, if we could go to the second page, please, in the paragraph numbered 2, if we could just highlight that, if there was a spelling error of the name Landzo, it seems to have been corrected there. Your Honours, there is another aspect of this document which we say is relevant, and it relates to the -- under the heading "statement of reason", that very first paragraph, if we could see the whole of that paragraph, the relevant part is starting in the middle of the first sentence: "Criminal charges brought by the command of the 4th Army Corps of the army of RBH, reference number POV05-149/92, dated 22nd December 1992." Your Honours, Exhibit 137, if that can be displayed on the screen, was the document that was admitted into evidence by the witness Pasalic. It is signed by him, it has been accepted into evidence and it relates in our submission to Exhibit 128 directly, and if we could quickly move to Exhibit 141, at the very top of the page of Exhibit 141, your Honours see on the left-hand side, right at the very top, that number that I just referred you to in Exhibit 128, the number POV05/149-92, 22nd December 1992 in Mostar. In our submission, your Honours, these two documents are related to each other, they deal with that one topic. The Prosecution emphasises it is not seeking to tender them for any other purpose than to show command responsibility and we submit that this document is a document that is on its face an authentic document by reference to its contents and to other documents. Again, it is a document that should be admitted into evidence. If I can move on to the next document, document 129, document 129 is again one of the documents in the series of documents relating to the investigations that were carried out in which certain persons in the area, including the accused Delalic, was said to be involved, but ultimately exonerated entirely, but it related to an incident that occurred in a place called Repovci. This is an analytical document. With this document, your Honours, I have not volunteered to extract the parts which we are not relying on, on the basis that I do believe, your Honours, you are not a jury, you are trained and that you are able, quite satisfactorily, to disregard all those parts of it which are not relied upon by the Prosecution or the Defence, and that it should not be necessary to go to that end, but if it is at the end of the day considered that in relation particularly to this document whether that is the course that should be admitted, I am prepared to undertake to do that, but I would submit, your Honours, that it is hardly necessary. We do submit that the document is very instructive of the role that was being played by the accused Zejnil Delalic at the relevant times mentioned in the document and indeed in the early periods, and in relation to that, we believe, your Honour, that this document is therefore relevant and admissible. The first page of the document, at the very top, merely puts it in context, the report is written about the period 12th July, it relates to an incident that happened at Repovci/Bradina road at a place called Savina Poda. It says, "A BH army military patrol was ambushed by persons unknown". It says: "Zejnil Delalic, army co-ordinator Konjic area, had ordered them to detain Sefik Ajanovic." By way of explanation and why we say this is relevant is that in our submission this document deals with an incident where certain police officers were ambushed on the road and killed. It is a document that analyses this incident. The persons, the police officers were there because of an order issued by the accused Zejnil Delalic. We are not suggesting we would in any way ask your Honours to infer anything by that, other than that he gave an order for this to happen. From a detailed reading of the document, the background is simply that there had been difficulty with certain members of the military to comply with orders, so the accused Delalic orders their arrest. The police contingent that goes up to effect that arrest were killed and that is what the nature of this report is. I only say that by way of background, so it can be understood in connection with that. What had also happened is because of the difficulties with the people failing to comply with the orders that were being issued, there is a process set in train in order for a new command to take over of that particular military group, and the reason why we seek to tender it is because it shows the role of the accused, Zejnil Delalic, in the establishment of that new command. If we could go to page 4 of the document, the second paragraph -- so, your Honours, we have reached the point where there was a necessity for a new command to be established. This paragraph here deals with that issue. It speaks of -- they also ask for another unit to be set up with personnel not engaged at the Bradina checkpoint and, if possible, people from the Konjic headquarters of the TO to come and discuss the problems. There was a meeting and it was concluded a new unit should be formed. It goes on: "The minutes from the meeting were taken by Demal Ferhatbegovic and Sefik Ajanovic on 10th July 1992 to the command building, the house of Zejnil Delalic, and they demanded that the minutes be sent on to Zvekusa village where Zejnil Delalic was with his staff at the time, because of combat operations against Chetniks et cetera et cetera in the Glabaticevo and Borci village area. On the same day Alija Avdibegovic and Azim Manduka came to the aforementioned command building, with a written appeal to Zejnil Delalic giving their view of the problem." We go to this because again we submit it points to his role in the area and the extent of his role in the area. The next paragraph on that page 4: "On 11th July 1992 at Mount Zvekusa", they went to see Zejnil Delalic. The same day the TO military police received the order from Delalic to carry out this arrest that I spoke of. Then significantly, we say, your Honours, it goes on: "... and detain them in Celebici prison for obstructing the work of the detachment. The military police were unable to carry out the order." Then the next paragraph: "At the very beginning of the war, in May 1992, the HVO and the TO forces took a building on Mount Zlatar, equipped with the most sophisticated communication systems." The taking of this building is something that is referred to again in this document. Then there is a reference, your Honours, in the final paragraph on that page: "From the beginning of the war until the events on the Repovci/Bradina road, the Konjic armed forces had had several successful operations (the take-over of the Celebici and Ljuta barracks)..." Your Honour Judge Jan once asked me what was the significance of Ljuta barracks and here is a reference to it: "... the active combat operations in the eastern part of the municipality). At the time, the War Presidency was acting as the organ of the civilian authority led by Dr Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic and Jasmin Guska, who was the chief of the Konjic SJB public security section. The Konjic TO HQ was headed by Esad Ramic, while the key figure was Zejnil Delalic as the ARBH co-ordinator." Again, your Honours, in our submission this goes to that question of the role that he played. It is the reference to the fact that the key figure, illustrated by the previous document with the railway, shows in our submission that he played a significant role of co-ordinator and was not just the role of having no command as such. Again, that is the reason why we say it is a relevant document. Over the page, on page 5 of this document, the very last sentence of the first paragraph, again a reference to the deterioration of relations between the HVO and Zejnil Delalic. It says: "A few days before the events in Repovci, he ordered a broadcast to be aired on Konjic Radio, claiming that a criminal report was to be filed against the HVO and against its leadership because of their obstructive behaviour in looting." I refer to this, your Honours, because your Honours will recall in document 126 that we looked at earlier, there was a document in 1993 and the question is, what of its relevance? In my submission, there is again a reference to broadcasting publicly the failure of the HVO to co-operate and to make it known to the public. This is a similar theme, in our submission, and one which obviously occurred right back at this early period and again was a theme that was suggested as an approach which we would say was suggested by the accused Delalic in dealing with this dispute with the HVO. Then again a reference to it in the next paragraph that follows that second sentence: "On 11th July 1992, the situation led to Zejnil Delalic ordering Konjic Radio to broadcast the information that members of the Konjic SJB were not taking part in combat operations but were involved in criminal activities." This in our submission is a relevant consideration. We have videos of the accused appearing on television in Croatia, again explaining the events that are happening, and so, your Honours, we say there is a thread there, a link there that shows that this is part of the approach taken by the accused in dealing with the events that were emerging in the area. We are not suggesting anything sinister at all by it, it is a perfectly appropriate legitimate approach, but all we are saying is there is a consistency which lends support to the reliability of this material. Again, on the same page, third paragraph from the bottom, there is a reference to the same question that was dealt with in Exhibit 126, that is the 1993, the April 1993 document, in our submission, where it says: "Operational data from that time indicated that there was an accord between the HVO forces and the Chetniks on the division of the Neretva valley, on the left bank Chetnik side, on the right bank Croatia side. This claim was corroborated by the HVO actions which led to the destruction of the bridges across the Neretva river and by the absence of their forces in the continuing combat actions against the Chetniks." Your Honours saw that expressed as alternatively an agreement between Boban and Karadzic or Tudjman and Milosevic. In our submission, your Honour, it is the same consistent thing that one sees time and time again. There is again on page 9, and I will not labour the issue again, other than to simply say that on page 9 of this particular document there is a reference to the characters that played significant roles in these events at those relevant times, the accused Zejnil Delalic, Jasmin Guska, the chief of the Konjic SJB and the President of the War Presidency, Dr Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic. Finally, perhaps I should refer to the final page, page 15, where at the very top of the page, the reference to the agreement between the Croatians and the Serbs is referred to as an agreement by Milosevic and Tudjman. On those bases, your Honours, and having regard to the relevance of that document, it is our submission that this is a document that should also be admitted into evidence. Now if we may move on to the next document, document 130. Your Honour, document 130 is a typewritten document, and we submit that this document was written by the accused Mucic. We say that and if we can go immediately to it, we say that firstly because of the nature of the way it has been signed at the very end of the document. This is a document that was taken -- care was taken with this document to verify its authenticity by the person that signed it. It was taken to the Consulate and before a consul of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the indictment was signed in Vienna by the accused Mucic in person, as it is attested there. On the original version of the document that was seized at the premises, there appears the stamp of the consul. There is also a reference there that your Honours can see to the passport that was issued by the public security station in Konjic on 7/12/1990. It is a very important document, your Honours, it is a document -- from the point of view of the Prosecution. It is a document that was addressed to the commander of the 4th Corps staff Mostar. I should, sorry, withdraw that, to the 4th Corps staff Mostar, municipal defence staff in Konjic. It is headed, "military secret, highly confidential", and it is a report. Your Honours, this document is a detailed report of the incidents that occurred during the year 1992 in the area of Konjic. It describes the roles played in various of the activities by the accused Mucic and by the accused Delalic. It is a document which from its reading presents itself as a memorandum designed, in our submission, to distance the accused Mucic from certain events that were being alleged against him at that time in relation to investigations that were being conducted in Mostar and Konjic against not only the accused Delalic but Mucic himself. It makes reference to that in the very early part of the document. It says in the very first paragraph: "Having read the press allegations", and I have on numerous occasions taken your Honours to references to that, "the commanding officer of Tactical Group 1 and to a certain extent myself, I wish to expose those fabrications and inform you as follows." Your Honours, in my submission I have shown you in particular Exhibits 137 and 141 and 117, where there are references to the fact that the Croatian press in particular fabricated stories about what the accused Delalic, and to a lesser extent Mucic, were doing. Your Honours, this document, to illustrate its relevance, I have to take you to it in some detail. Dealing firstly with the second sentence in the first paragraph , numbered 1, it says: "Problems with the BH army and other bodies in the municipality of Konjic started on the day that Zejnil Delalic had to hand over command of the Konjic forces to other commanding officers and heads of departments, having been appointed to a higher post than that of commanding officer of Tactical Group 1, based on Pazaric, Konjic, Jablanica, Prozor, on the Mount of Igman and other places I am not aware of." Your Honours, in our submission, this relates to the handing over of command when the 4th Corps finally is set up. It is a criticism of that: "All the successfully planned and carried-out operations in Konjic, from the very beginning of the war, were done while he", in our submission Zejnil Delalic, "was the leader in Konjic. In brief, since I have been involved from the very beginning." In our submission, your Honour, this goes to show that the accused Mucic, who was there in the very beginning, he even shows that, is well placed to then go on and describe these events. He goes on in the second paragraph from the bottom, starting: "At the very beginning, the HVO was treated as a paramilitary organisation and encountered problems with the municipal bodies, and even ordinary people, because the BH leadership had not yet taken a clear stand about the uprising and had not clearly labelled the aggressor." That in our submission is a reference to this ongoing conflict that existed with the HVO: "He", and again we say this means the accused Delalic, "put his and his sister's house at the disposal of the BH-Army and the HVO." Previously I had taken your Honours to an exhibit where there was this meeting at the commander's house and we submit, your Honour, that that relates to that particular thing, to that issue, and again, that is referred to in Exhibit 129. Going on: "Investing his authority, reputation and extraordinary organisational skills, Zejnil", in our submission Zejnil Delalic, "managed to overcome the Muslim lethargy and to achieve regular army status for the HVO in Konjic. I myself was a member of that army. The very first money received by the HVO treasury was Zejnil's money." Your Honours will recall, you have looked at exhibits but in particular exhibit I think 144, where a document which is signed "Zejnil Delalic, Commander of Tactical Group 1". There is a reference there in that document to the fact that he had contributed considerable sums of money to the army in Bosnia-Herzegovina in its early days and its early establishment. I am sorry, page 3, was that reference? If we could go to 144, page 3, we see there the reference in the second from the bottom: "I bought 2,000 uniforms", et cetera, "the remaining communications equipment with my own money." But then goes, if we may go back to document 120 at that bottom paragraph, -- sorry, 130, bottom paragraph. It then goes on in the middle of that paragraph: "I was employed in Austria." That is where the accused Mucic was arrested, your Honours are aware of that: "I used to bring over the money." He goes on to talk about the amounts, which I do not need to trouble your Honours with. He goes on in the next sentence: "I know he had spent all the money by May 1992, for the army in Konjic and other places. People would come from all the regions in order to manage and get through to reach him." Your Honours recall those exhibits which we put in, they were in very scribbled handwriting, but they deal, we submit, deal with the purchasing of arms and matters we showed you earlier. We submit this goes to those questions as well. Going over now to the top of the next page, it starts off, the very top paragraph: "He", we submit Zejnil Delalic again, "was strict and severe and his orders were immediately carried out, although some people were already beginning to hate him, but the achievements were proving his point." It then goes on: "As early as 19th April, the first group of select volunteers, myself included, occupied the barracks in Celebici and the Serbian village itself. Those were the first barracks in BH to fall. There were about 20 of us. We were poorly armed. Zejnil rode in the leading car, carrying a Kalasnikov, purchased with his own money. All the big HVO and TO and MUP bosses stayed in Zejnil's house in Konjic, waiting to see whether we would come back alive or not." Your Honours, in Exhibit 144, on page 4, and if I can go to that, please, at the bottom paragraph, again, this is a document that I said earlier is signed "Zejnil Delalic, Commander of Tactical Group 1", it says: "I was in Konjic until the end of June. I took part in all actions, including the seizure of the Celebici barracks. It was the first barracks to be taken in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was a leader of a group of about 20 volunteers. The leaders of the TO, HVO and MUP were waiting in my house for the outcome of the operations. It was on 19th April 1992." In our submission, your Honours, it is almost word for word what appears in Exhibit 130. Then going down that -- if I can go back now, please, to Exhibit 130, then going down that same paragraph entitled "(a)", in the second to last sentence, third to last sentence, it starts: "Zejnil", in our submission Zejnil Delalic, "ordered that one of our groups move into the barracks that very night and adapt them for a future prison or war camp".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Where is this portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. If your Honour looks on your television screen, it is six lines from the bottom of the first paragraph, paragraph (a), starting "Zejnil ordered", where the marker is now showing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes. The thread has still not got --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sorry, perhaps the marker could be on -- do you see where the marker is on the side, your Honour: "Zejnil ordered that one of our groups move into the barracks that very night and adapt them for a future prison or war camp".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next paragraph immediately beneath that makes reference to an event that occurred in the Igman armament factory. It says: "A few days later, the captured weapons were utilised to take the Igman armament factory and a substantial quantity of weapons, especially the anti-aircraft guns, that were immediately taken out and installed and brought down their first planes the very next day." Your Honours, this is just an event, but it is an event which we submit relates to an event that was participated in by the accused Delalic in his capacity at that time, and it is referred to in a video Exhibit 116, which we will go to in due course. But it is confirmed by that. Down the bottom of the page, in the paragraph commencing "(c)", there is relation to an operation in "D Selo". If I recall, I think your Honours at one stage asked me what a particular exhibit that made reference to "D Selo" meant; it was Exhibit 119 and if it can quickly be put on the screen, Exhibit 119, and blown up, your Honours will see the reference there "Dugo Selo barracks" and down in paragraph 4, a reference to the accused Mucic and it is signed, "Commander Zejnil Delalic" and in Zagreb, him being in Zagreb in the early part of May. If we may go over the page on to page 3, in paragraph (d) towards the bottom of the page, there is a reference there to military activity. It says: "Two weeks later Zejnil organised and commanded jointly with Mr. Zovko (HVO) the Bradina operation, HVO 1 battalion joined the operation on the second day. Results: Communications between Konjic and Hadzici were re-established and Bradina was taken in two days." Again, just another reference to the activities and his particular involvement at the time. Towards the bottom of the page, a note appears on the document. It says: "The usual practice in both locations was that the group or unit which captured any armaments would keep them and use them to arm its new members. During the interrogation in prison, detainees would also admit the existence of weapons' caches. Most of them had extra weapons buried near their houses ..." Going over the page: "... and would be taken by the MUP patrols to show the exact locations. All such armaments were taken and stored by the MUP. Everybody knows that Zejnil", in our submission Zejnil Delalic, "continuously argued with Guska about that and about the poor participation of MUP reserve units in the operations. The quarrels escalated after the withdrawal of the HVO and the joint command in June 1992. Zejnil", Delalic in our submission, "insisted that every weapon found be given to new members of the BH-Army." Your Honours, in our submission this goes to show that the accused Delalic knew that interrogation of prisoners was taking place, it goes to show that the purpose of the interrogation, one of the purposes of the interrogation, was to locate weapons, and for those weapons to then be distributed to members of the BH-Army, and is again consistent with what I have said about that April 1993 document, where it speaks of a similar modus operandi in relation to any attack on the HVO. Your Honours, also it is a matter which is referred to in Exhibit 129. If we go to the very bottom of the page, your Honours, on that page, we see that short paragraph I showed you relating to the rail transport: "Five days later, quite on his own, he organised the first rail transport along", et cetera. I was referring your Honours to Exhibit 127. Then paragraph (f): "Delalic insisted that we attack Borci a week after Bradina, and that the entire municipality be cleansed. However, it could not be done because the HVO withdrew." I took your Honours to that part which showed the dispute then developed between the accused. Over the page, page 5, there is a reference there right in the very centre of the very last paragraph, the big long paragraph, there is a reference I just draw your Honours' attention to, I do not need to go to it in detail, but a reference to the Repovci incident where the police officers were ambushed and killed, which I referred your Honours to earlier. Over the page, on page 6, there is again further reference to it, and in the last sentence of the top paragraph, the accused Mucic says that Zejnil's Delalic's involvement in this particular crime would be an absurd thing, because of the fact that previously his brother was believed to also have been among the police officers that were killed. We do not need to go into that, it is just it is consistent again with that pattern. Then your Honours, in the second to last sentence of that paragraph in the middle of the page, starting: "In any case, several members of the military command of the armed forces managed to get out of Sarajevo, attempted in vain to consolidate the ranks and led to quite numerous and well armed Konjic army battles of Borci and Mt. Igman. The result was drawing attention to themselves and stupid investigation primarily detrimental to the BH-Army." Again, just a reference to these ongoing investigations that occurred, the next paragraph, starting, "I am surprised", there is a reference there to the media. It says: "Judging by the media, it is obvious that both the other hostile sides respected Zejnil more than the BH-Army." Finally on this page: "In Austria, where my wife and children have found refuge, I have attempted recently to get in touch with Mr. Delalic, but have not been received. He thinks when I was commanding the prison, I made various mistakes that he is now held responsible for, at least by the media. After all, everybody knows that the first person to be declared a war criminal by Serbian BH and Serbia proper was Zejnil, at the end of April 1992." I notice, your Honours, it is 11.30. I still have some more references to this document that I wish to take you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will have a short break. At 12.00 we will continue on that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, what is the date of this letter? I do not find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is a date that appears on it, your Honour, but it does not -- it is left blank. I am sorry your Honour, there is no date on it. It is only something that from its contents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is signed by the writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at that. I thought maybe the date was shown there, but it is not shown there either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it signed, the one you have with you, the one which was allegedly recovered from INDA-BAU?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I may be able to call that up on the screen, perhaps page 12 of the Bosnian version, could that be put on the screen, please? There does not appear to be a date. Could that bottom section be highlighted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This merely is a reference to the date on which the identity card was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It is not the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was looking at this letter. Does it bear any signatures, this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what is showing on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: No, this is probably the document further on, the letter to the consul attesting his ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is page 12, but it is the document we were referring to. This is the Bosnian version of it. There does not appear to be a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is all right. You may continue. I see Mr. Ackerman is on his feet. Let us hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a matter I need to bring to your attention, your Honours. With regard to Mr. Landzo, I have now received the report from Mr. Heinz. It is brief and fairly cryptic. I must supplement that information with a report that the authorities at the detention unit have instructed Mr. Landzo that he must be there in the morning to see the psychiatrist, because of what happened the night before last. It now gives me some concern that at least someone believes it may have been something more than accidental. I believe not, but someone apparently does believe that. I raised that issue with the Registry before we had the break, and had been informed that it is possible to reschedule that meeting with the psychiatrist on Friday, so that it would not interrupt our being in session on Thursday. The only concern I have about that, and I am not sure it is a real concern, but it is one that I have, is that if whoever at the detention unit has decided that he needs to see a psychiatrist tomorrow has based that upon information that I am not privy to, then there is a conflict with regard to the information that I have received, and I would not want to take responsibility myself for anything that could happen between now and Friday with regard to Mr. Landzo. I am perfectly happy for him to see the psychiatrist on Friday, that probably is the best solution, but I am concerned that if there is a basis for the concern that it is something that ought to be dealt with sooner rather than later before someone has to take responsibility for something untoward that could occur. I am at a loss. I do not have a solution, but I do not want to personally take responsibility for requesting that the psychiatrist's visit be put off until Friday. I will accept the views of the Trial Chamber, however, without objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ackerman. The Trial Chamber is very concerned about Mr. Landzo's health. He has had a few difficulties and as a young man could be the child of any of us, and we think it is important that his health should be given proper attention. I do not know whether he, Landzo, would be able to co-operate with us in these circumstances to kindly give an undertaking that he will be able to attend the psychiatrist on Friday. It is only a day between. I agree 24 hours means quite a lot with a person's health, but I think it is our concern for his health and as much as possible we can give him as much help and assistance as we can, if he also will co-operate with us and attend the psychiatrist's examination on Friday, because that is only between tomorrow and the next day. That will not be a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I can tell you that Mr. Landzo is perfectly willing to wait until Friday to see the psychiatrist. My only concern about that would be: does he possess the competency to make that decision? I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just again want to express my own concern that I do not want to take responsibility for it being put off until Friday based upon the minimal information that I have right now. Someone at the detention centre apparently thinks it is important that he see the psychiatrist tomorrow. I do not even know who that is. If it is a guard, then I am not very concerned. If it is one of the medical personnel there then I am; I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are not trying to deny responsibility for rescheduling, we are only relying on his courage and his composure and ability to know how long he can carry on before he sees the medical personnel and I think he will be able to cope between now and Friday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just have a note from Mr. Landzo which says: "Tomorrow coming prison doctor. Because of that I must see doctor tomorrow." I think perhaps Mr. Landzo does not understand that the detention centre has indicated that it is possible to reschedule this doctor until Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will give him every co-operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do want to say, your Honour, that I appreciate your concern for Mr. Landzo's condition. He and I both appreciate that and I leave it in your hands as to whether he see the doctor tomorrow or Friday. It is a decision that I do not feel competent to make, because I have insufficient information to make that decision. But Mr. Landzo himself does not object to waiting until Friday to see the doctor, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. (Pause). Thank you very much. I think the Trial Chamber thinks Friday might be a more convenient day for everyone and we will make sure that even today if there is any necessity, I think we can pressurise; if it is needed to do so we can do so, instead of waiting for that long. Thank you very much. Mr. Niemann, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. If we could move on to page 7 of the English version of this document, please? Top paragraph, your Honours, is entitled with a heading, "Prisoners and camps in Konjic". It starts by saying: "Let me emphasise at the very beginning that any miscarriages and irregularities in that respect alleged by local slander and bombastic stories in the Croatian press could only be ascribed to me as the prison commander and my deputy and other co-workers in the prison and further to persons in the municipality." The next paragraph, your Honour sees: "Zejnil had nothing to do with any prisoners. He only liberated the barracks, established the prison and was the first in BH to classify the prisoners in nine categories while he was in charge only of Konjic. On the contrary, apart from achieving all that, he also filled the prison with 500 Serbs and Chetniks. A further 200 prisoners, mainly civilian Serbs, were brought in by others." Your Honours, in our submission, the relevance of this is that it goes to the question of the application of the Conventions, the Geneva Conventions, to the persons detained in the prison and for the reason why they were incarcerated there. It then goes on: "This category was chiefly brought in because of private disputes, even old ones from before the war. At one time, at the very beginning, I had almost 700 prisoners. After the fall of Bradina, we encountered various problems, including lack of food, guards and medical care." These are all matters that your Honours have heard of in the course of the testimony of the witnesses: "Among the less significant information that I wish to bring to your attention is the fact that all the shovel handles in Celebici were broken in two days because the new prisoners were beaten, irrespective of the degree of their guilt. We had a lot of problems with seriously injured prisoners. Many of them died, and we caused ourselves additional trouble as we had to provide medical care et cetera because a Geneva team registered the camp very soon after. The three member commissions were set up to carry out the first interrogation and to categorise the prisoners." Then it goes on to refer to the commission. The next paragraph commences: "Discharged on 18th November 1992 from my post as prison commander, I duly handed over to my successor all the reports and lists of all the commissions and all the categories. Therefore up to the arrival of the state commission, decisions on the release of the wrongfully detained Serbian nationals were made by Mr. Goran Lokas." He goes on to deal with that issue. Your Honours, in Exhibit 131, which we will come to next, and perhaps if I can just make reference to it now, the second page of the English translation, if that could be blown up there, this document, your Honours, as I say which we will come to next, was also a document found among these documents in Vienna and in particular, in our submission, there is a relationship between documents 130 and 131, at least in this context, where it says there: "Within the framework of the transfer of duties carried out by TG1, all responsibilities, the warehouses, prisons et cetera were transferred in an orderly fashion. In this context, I want to point out that the Celebici prison was handed over to the Konjic Ops/OS ... as early as 15th November 1992, at which point the prison commander Pavo, who had been in that post until then, was replaced and relieved of his duties." I do note, your Honours, and just so it is not said otherwise, that the dates seem to be different. The dates in Exhibit 131 of the handover, it speaks of as early as 15th November 1992, at which point the prison commander had been replaced, and in the document 130, the date referred to is 18th November. But it is our submission that very little turns on that. Your Honours, going back to Exhibit 130, page 7, the very bottom of the page , there is a reference there again to the fact that Mr. Delalic had not personally communicated with any of the prisoners or carried out any interrogation, which is consistent with the Prosecution case. Page 8, if we may go over to that, it explains, in our submission, the top paragraph, why it is that the accused Delalic was not involved in such things as interrogation of prisoners, when it says at the top of that page: "Busy with the more important matters, once the prison had been established, he seldom visited it, except when escorting delegations of other BH command posts, the press and the Geneva Red Cross." Your Honours have heard evidence I think of those visits, particularly his involvement with the Geneva Red Cross: "On those occasions, he would mostly check on the work of the investigation commissions, accommodation conditions, appearance of the guards and whether the treatment of inmates conformed to the Geneva Convention." The next paragraph: "All the work on the exchange of prisoners and the release of prisoners in all-for-all exchanges were performed by Ms. J Dzumhur, myself and my deputy. The military police provided the necessary escort and monitored the implementation of agreed exchanges. The TG1 command reprimanded us on several occasions because of irregularities in the implementation procedure. The last order we received from the main state commission in Sarajevo before the expiration of my mandate was to release 134 prisoners unconditionally." It goes on, your Honours, then two paragraphs -- one paragraph further down, commencing: "Allegedly, three persons were supposed to have been killed in the prison. That is not true, because over 30 prisoners had died there because of various reasons. One single shell exploding in the sports centre killed 14 Serbs, and wounded several guards." Your Honours, this appears to be a reference to Musala prison, and your Honours will recall that the heading of this document relates to, "Prisoners and camps in Konjic", as opposed to being limited to Celebici camp. It then goes on, significantly, your Honour, in that sentence, in terms of why we say this is a relevant document: "The rest succumbed to beatings, injuries, or were killed while attempting to escape, or died of natural causes. A general chaos prevailed in the beginning. Various civilians and members of the MUP would come in and beat the prisoners up. At the same time, other Muslims and Croat civilians would bring food and cigarettes to Serbs, their former neighbours and acquaintances. It all went on until I brought some order and strengthened the guard and security system. Hazim Delic, my deputy, and Mitke, commanding officer of the sabotage and reconnaissance unit, arranged to move to one of the prison rooms one of their number (a man called Hodza) who had syphilis and who had previously been housed in the motel." It goes on: "Delalic could not and should not have known we were housing the sick men and the allegations about the order for his murder were nothing but fabrications. The orders about anything connected with the prison were received and passed on only and exclusively by me. Commanding officer Delalic never gave such an order to anybody." Your Honours, in my submission, that relates to the order to murder this person which the investigations were about and which in our submission this memorandum is addressed to correct, in part at least, so it says: "Commanding officer Delalic never gave such an order to anybody", namely an order to carry out a murder. "Any discrepancies about the case should be clarified by Hazim and Mitke and it should be investigated whether it was a case of murder of a sick man or a case of death due to natural causes as diagnosed by the doctor." Again, the relevance of that is just to that question of the murder. We say the significance of this particular paragraph is the reference to Commanding Officer Delalic and giving orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to interrupt my learned friend, I am sure he will forgive me when he hears the reason for it. This is a reference to the matter that the Prosecution has already said they do not rely on. Does he now change his stance on that? This matter involving Hodza who had syphilis is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am indebted to my friend. I am not in any way wishing to bring this matter into the Chamber as a matter for your Honours' consideration, I was merely wishing to explain any ambiguity that might appear in the sentence: "Commanding officer Delalic never gave such an order to anybody." I believe it is open to ambiguity, and I was endeavouring to address that issue of ambiguity, should there be any, but I am certainly not in any way wishing to ask your Honours to have regard or consider that issue. Your Honours, at the very bottom of the page, there is a reference again to "D Selo", which I had taken your Honours to at least one document that related to that, and the author of this, the accused Mucic, in our submission, then goes on to say: "My departure was only known to my deputy", this is the very last sentence, "who was under orders to shoot 100 imprisoned Serbs if I failed to return within a prearranged time." Again, your Honours, we submit that this is an issue that goes to the question of dealing with people who are imprisoned, it is evidence of the fact that not only were they imprisoned so that arms could be obtained from them, not only were they imprisoned so that they could be demobilised or rendered defective in terms of the Serbs, but there was another and more sinister motive, and it goes along with the issue of exchange, that these prisoners could in fact be held hostage if events dictated it. We are not suggesting that that happened, but we are saying this is another motive for it. We submit that it is a relevant matter for your Honours' consideration. In the next paragraph on page 9, it goes on: "I had not requested permission for my trip from the commanding officer of TG1 Konjic ..." So he had not sought permission to do this from TG1 Konjic or from the Ops/OS: "... nor had I informed them of my intentions, but I did report to them my findings. Delalic told me that J Dzumhur, the chairman of the state commission, should be informed urgently, and that an official report should be made immediately to MUP Konjic because civilians were involved and the territory was controlled by the Konjic MUP. All that happened early in October." Skipping one paragraph and going down: "Talking about the investigations and the situation with the prison commissions and Celebici, I can say that many errors were made when determining the categories. Individual groups were governed by who knows whose instructions and judgements. In my opinion, as I have already stated in my last transfer of duty report, there are only 11 cases who cannot be either exchanged or released. I have made a list of their names. Although I kept pointing out to Konjic municipal headquarters that no charges had been raised, not even repeated interventions by the International Red Cross brought any results. I complained to TG1 command and they issued several written warnings about the situation." It goes on. Moving on to the next paragraph: "As to the alleged release of 270 Chetniks, most of whom I would consider simply Serbian nationals, I wish to specify that the total of 300 Serbs and Chetniks were released." It goes on, and then finally: "Under full moral, personal and military responsibility, I state as an irrefutable fact that except in retrospect, the TG1 commander Mr. Zejnil Delalic had no knowledge of these events nor ordered nor approved anything. On the contrary, he criticised me severely, as can be attested to by his deputy Saric, who was present when I talked about it." This document, your Honour, is the one that then goes on and is signed and the signature is attested to by the Consulate for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Vienna. Your Honour, the next document, if it may be brought on to the screen, Exhibit 131. This document, your Honours, is again a hand-written note, and it is not signed and nor is it dated, but in our submission, from reading of the document, the period of time of when it happens to have been brought into existence can be ascertained insofar as at least it relates to the period of time following the departure of the accused Mucic and Delalic from Konjic in November 1992. Again, this document was found on the premises of INDA-BAU. When it was presented to Mr. Moerbauer, in the course of his evidence, at page 3654, at lines 7 to 8, Moerbauer said of the document: "This was in binder I6 and was handed to me at the Vienna police headquarters by my colleague, Navrat." The document, your Honours, is a document which we submit is a reliable document and could be admitted into evidence and can be admitted into evidence because of its contents and what it purports to set out. It is a similar document to the last document that we looked at, the document that was written by the accused Mucic, similar in the sense that it is a document which we submit is the kind, or of a class, which may be retained by someone who was wishing to provide an explanation by various sources of their involvement in certain events, or their non-involvement in certain events, and why it is that it might be said that whatever has been alleged against that person, in this case Delalic, was unjustified. Your Honours, this document was a document we say was, if not written by the deputy of the accused Delalic, as it may well not have been written by him, it is certainly written as if it was a document created by him, but it relates to the accused Delalic. It starts: "I was the deputy to the commander of TG1 (Tactical Group 1), Zejnil Delalic." The reference to that person, who the deputy was, I have taken your Honours to it in a number of other documents, but in one of the documents that I took your Honours to, was document 132, which we will come to shortly. I will deal with it in much greater detail when we come to it, but it is also a document that is at least said to have been written by Edib Saric, who we submit was the deputy commander of the accused Delalic, and also, your Honours, document 137. If we can just go to document 137 for a moment, please, that document, the person listed there as number 1 is described as, "assistant to the commander of TG1 for security". This document, as your Honours know, was admitted and has been accepted into evidence through the witness Pasalic. So, your Honours, this document, as I say, goes on to provide and we say is relevant because it does so -- this person says he was the deputy of the accused Delalic on the day that the accused left, at around 8.00 pm on 25th November 1992. Your Honours will remember the numerous documents that I took you to where that particular time and date has been stated as the date on which the accused Delalic left the Konjic area and went via Croatia into Austria. It is also a matter that was attested to by the witness Pasalic.
