The document goes on in the first paragraph: "The departure was planned in a completely regular way, because with the establishment of the 4th Corps, TG1 had practically ceased to exist, except for the completion of certain administrative work which I was supposed to finish." Your Honours will recall in Exhibit 117 that the document was signed in the name "Delalic", which was also hand-written and found on the premises -- I withdraw that, your Honour. It was not signed. I withdraw that. In document 117 there is a reference at the very bottom of the first page, I do not need to take your Honours to it, it simply says: "With the establishment of the 4th Corps Mostar and the one Sarajevo Corps already established, my former zone of responsibility was covered, so in the middle of November it was concluded that TG1 should be dissolved." That is document 117 which your Honours have already considered. We submit that is consistent again with what is written here. It says: "Even though 4th Corps was officially established on 24th November 1992, Zejnil only left on 25th November 1992." It goes on in the next paragraph: "In particular, A Pasalic knew of it and in my presence he warned him of a potential ambush on the way through Herzegovina. With that in mind, Arif gave him some certificates." Again, your Honours, in Exhibit 117, there is a reference there to Colonel Pasalic, when he says at the top of the page: "That is why I still have not fully comprehended some of his moves following my departure. Persons who knew about my travel plans were first Colonel Pasalic", and then he goes on to name others. At the bottom of that paragraph on that first page of this document, there is a reference to this coming to him: "... with a cellular phone, so I immediately tried to call numbers in Zagreb and Vienna that Zejnil had left with me. I got through and from that day, all the way up until the turmoil of our arrests in early December", and I have taken your Honours to the document where the witness Pasalic ordered that Edib Saric be arrested, "I talked to him every day, several times a day." Your Honours, in Exhibit 124, and if we could perhaps just have that for a moment on the screen, page 2 of Exhibit 124 if we may, it is four paragraphs from the top, starts, "at about 1400 hours". Your Honours might see the marker that is shown on the screen there which indicates the paragraph I am referring to: "At about 1400 hours, across the border into Austria. Luckily I have the stamp in my passport", and so forth: "The next day I had a call on a mobile phone from Saric. I used the occasion to explain everything that remained to be explained." Your Honours, turning over the page, the second page of document 131, if we could, please, the first two sentences refer to the issue of the travel, and then there is the sentence: "The official invitation to visit our clubs in CH", your Honours may be aware of "CH" being initials or abbreviations used in Europe to make reference to Switzerland, "and other countries came from Sadic, who is the President's right hand man." Your Honours, in Exhibit 131, when we were looking at this exhibit -- sorry, Exhibit 132 -- there is a reference in our submission there to this question again, and if we could just go to the first page of Exhibit 132 -- I may have to come back to that. I do apologise, it is the final page, third paragraph from the bottom: "You asked him to give lectures in the clubs for our people, collect funds and work on information and propaganda activities, which are in a poor state at the moment." This is a letter again written by or signed by Saric, Edib Saric, and is addressed to the President, presumably the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, your Honours, we move on to the part of the document which in our submission is the very relevant part of this document, so Exhibit 131, this is the second page we are looking at: "Within the framework of the transfer, duties carried out by TG1, all key responsibilities, the warehouses" -- I have read this part of it to your Honours before: "In this context, I want to point out that Celebici prison was handed over", et cetera: "If Pavo also left on 25th November to work abroad then who escaped or deserted his post in the army, because he had already been relieved of his post", et cetera. Then, your Honours, there is written, and as I say, this is a hand-written document, there is written at the bottom of the document -- the document is ruled off in a sense, and perhaps if we could just see for a moment the Bosnian version of the document, can we see the last page, particularly that part headed "paradox". The very bottom part, your Honours see how the page is ruled off and then there appears Bosnian writing there. If we could go back again to the English version at that point, it says: "In the barracks which I personally liberated and turned into a camp for Serbs, there my brother and my associates are being imprisoned." Your Honours, in our submission this may be a matter that your Honours might well conclude indicates that in fact the author of this hand-written document was not Edib Saric at all, but indeed the accused Delalic. We say that because the reference to, "the barracks which I personally liberated", your Honours have seen references that I have taken you to where the accused Delalic participated in the taking of the barracks at Celebici. Your Honours have also seen references that I have taken you to where he ordered that it be turned into a camp and it says "a camp for Serbs", and that is indeed what it became. Then he says, it is under the title line "paradox": "There my brother and my associates are being imprisoned." Your Honours, in the document that is admitted into evidence by General Pasalic, document 137, if we can just have that again on the screen, your Honours will see in the persons that were to be detained, and your Honours have heard evidence that they were detained in the Celebici camp itself, you will see a reference there in number 12 to "ZA", and then in my translation it is not clear, but I believe there is a clearer version of this document, the original of this document, where the name Zahir, Z-A-H-I-R, would be made out and Zahir Delalic, in our submission, is that reference which is referred to as the brother of the accused Zejnil Delalic, and your Honours will see that there are also references to people who could well be described as his associates in that document. So in our submission, your Honours, it would seem from that that if that interpretation is correct, then the true author of the document is not Saric at all, although it would appear that that is the person who would present as the person who wrote it. It may well have been written by the accused Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is there any evidence that it is in his handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is no evidence of handwriting that your Honours have heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who is "Adventurer"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not able to assist your Honour with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Any guess?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can have a guess, your Honour. I can guess it is possibly a newspaper, and that this was being prepared for that purpose, but I am only guessing on that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I asked you for a guess because you are counsel, you are not a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in that connection it seems to me that things are getting a bit out of hand and that some line must be drawn between counsel making proffers of documents and counsel offering testimony to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is just presenting documents which he says have been found from the possession of the accused and he wants to tender them, explaining them. These are his arguments. Fair enough, admission and probative value are two different things. Probative value we have not yet determined, because there may be certain attending circumstances which may reduce the probative value, or which may make them not probative at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree with that, but with all due respect, he is going beyond that. He is telling you and has just told you that he has been able to make out that language in a document that is very difficult to read in fact says such and such and such and such. That is testimony, that is something we should be permitted to cross-examine him about, if he is permitted to testify about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Give a counter-argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is the kind of information that should come from a witness on the stand and not from counsel. It is evidentiary in nature. It is not a proffer, it is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, in relation to that I will make available the document I rely upon in order to make that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not think it is necessary. While determining the relevance of any document, you use also your skills before you decide whether a document is relevant. That might not be the same skills that might be used by the Trial Chamber while actually determining its evidence, so I do not see any quarrel with that. The Defence can also regard it as irrelevant or not a consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Or without probative value, including the attending circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You put up your arguments, then the Defence will also make its own arguments and we will consider it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They can also make their guesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, of course. Your Honours, if we can now move on, seeing as we have a few moments left, to the next document, document 132.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You concluded your view of 131?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the last document. I submit that is a document that has sufficient indicia of reliability, is very relevant and it is a document that should be admitted into evidence. Going on to document 132, if we may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually we should have a short break here and come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours. Your Honours, if we could have document 132 on the screen, please, the first page of that document. Your Honours, as I was saying just before the break, this document is in the form of a letter; it is in typewritten form and the name at the bottom is "Edib Saric", and then beneath that there is hand-written the words, "20th November 1992, sent by KT and receipt acknowledged by VK, supreme command." That is in handwriting, your Honours. This document was also found at the premises of INDA-BAU and when presented to Mr. Moerbauer at page 3654, lines 10 and 11 of his evidence, he said: "This was in binder I6 and was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at the Vienna police headquarters." Your Honours, this document is a document, as I said, about the accused Delalic. It speaks of his role during the period 1992, and it is a letter which is written in the style which suggests to be in favour of him, having regard to the allegations that were made against the accused Delalic. Your Honours, I have taken you to a number of documents where I have shown you that Edib Saric was a deputy or assistant to Zejnil Delalic, the accused, in his capacity of Tactical Group 1 commander. On the first page of the document, in the centre of the page, he says: "I would to write to you about such a man who became an institution because of everything that he did, because I am not in a position to tell you this personally. His name is Zejnil Delalic." Then he proceeds to set out details about Zejnil Delalic. He says, your Honours, a few lines down from that: "He has lived in the west for 20 years. He has an university education, speaks and reads and writes several foreign languages. He has his own companies in Austria, Switzerland, Belgium and Germany." A couple of lines down from that: "He came to his hometown in March to organise his neighbours and to prepare them for war. During that period, of all of us who were directed to Konjic, Zejnil was a man who gave advice and help." He goes on to speak of the fall of Bradina, how Konjic became a logistics centre, and how he used his own money to purchase equipment for the army. It then refers, "Sefer appointed him as commander of TG1." Your Honours will recall that in Exhibit 118, we have the appointment of the accused Delalic to the position of TG1 by Sefer Halilovic. There is then reference to his exceptional organisational abilities and so forth, on that page. There is a reference at the top of the next page, page 2, to his role with the HZ-HB Croatian Community. He talks of: "Implementing the orders issued by the chief of staff, Sefer", your Honours, in our submission that is a reference to Sefer Halilovic, "and sometimes issued by you." In our submission, your Honour, that is a reference to the President, Alija Izetbegovic. We say that, your Honour, there is a reference in Exhibit 124 along those lines, and if we could go momentarily please to Exhibit 124, on the second page at the very bottom of 124, down the bottom of the page, there is a reference there in the last sentence of the paragraph numbered 4: . "I had threatened him with the Sultan", I believe that is a large piece of artillery, "of course on the orders of my chief", I submit his chief is Sefer Halilovic, "and President Izetbegovic." Your Honours, in my submission that is a consistent reference which is picked up in this letter as well. Going back, your Honours, to Exhibit 132, you may, on page 2, there is a reference in the middle paragraph starting "Mr. President"; they both start Mr. President, but the middle paragraph. I should say the paragraph more to the top, "Mr. President, those people are representatives of our MUP", that paragraph. Going down to the centre of that paragraph, the sentence starting: "The chief sent him Jovan Divjak, an extraordinary man and warrior, who became only a burden in his area. Divjak can and must be more usefully engaged in Sarajevo", et cetera et cetera. Your Honour, this is in our submission a reference to when Divjak came out to Konjic and was there at the same time as the accused Delalic and you heard from Divjak when he testified to this when he travelled and arrived there. Then there is a reference in the very last sentence of that paragraph to Sefer again: "Sefer gave authority to Zejnil and Karic to reduce tensions with the HVO through negotiations and by forming joint commands." If we could move then on to the last page of the document, page 4, there is a reference there which I have previously taken your Honours to, the third paragraph down, "that you ask him to give lectures in the clubs for our people", et cetera. I referred you to it in Exhibit 131, where there is a reference to the fact that he was to give lectures in Switzerland and places outside Yugoslavia. So in combination, if your Honours please, it is our submission that this document has all the indicia of reliability; it is consistent with many other of the documents I have taken your Honours to, it complies with that central theme, and in our submission is reliable and should be admitted into evidence. Now, your Honours, moving on to the next document, if I may, Exhibit 133. Perhaps that could be displayed on the screen. Your Honour, this document is in the form of an identification card. It is headed "The Green Berets", and it bears the name of the accused, Zejnil Delalic, his father's name Salko and date of birth, refers to Konjic and it is dated 15th January 1992, and bears a registration number. This document was also found at the premises of INDA-BAU and Mr. Moerbauer, when shown this particular document, said at page 3654, lines 12 to 14: "This identity card was in binder I6 and was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at Vienna police headquarters." Your Honours, in the record of interview with the accused Delalic on 22nd August 1996, this Green Beret card was presented to the accused, and if I can just -- this is now in evidence as Exhibit 99, which has been tendered, your Honours. The investigator asked the question at pages 7 through to 9 about this particular document. He says: "At the time, were you a member of any kind of military organisation or military association, or any patriotic organisation?"

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED ANSWERED
utterances.text: "No, I was present at one meeting on the occasion of my New Year's visit. It was a kind of humanitarian organisation. Their name was something like the Green Berets, but they were just in the process of setting up the organisation, but I forgot about it. In April when the events took place, this organisation did not appear any more." The investigator then said: "I am now showing you a card, I suppose it is a membership card of the Green Berets." If your Honours please, it is a copy of the Exhibit 133 that I have just taken your Honours to. When it was presented to the accused, he said: "I got it in 1994 when I was in Vienna already. They were celebrating some anniversary, so they asked for some assistance, because they were in charge of children and disabled persons, war veterans, and I remember that some time around the New Year, they had their establishing meeting. I believe they came active and operational in 1993 and their task was to take care of children and persons killed in the war." Your Honours, in our submission, there is nothing there to suggest that the accused Zejnil Delalic, when presented with this document, a copy of which has been seized at the INDA-BAU premises in Vienna, there is nothing in the record of interview in any way to suggest that he said, "this was a forgery, it must have been placed among papers in order that someone may suggest that there are things about me which are not true". Not at all, he did not deny that it was a document that directly pertained to him. In our submission, your Honours, it is a document that goes to identification. The issue of Green Berets is another issue which may emerge during the course of the proceedings and in my submission, your Honours, the fact that not only was it found among these documents and as such bears indicia of reliability on that basis alone, and because it was found on the premises is relevant and admissible, but it is also relevant and admissible because it has been shown to the accused and he did not deny that it was his document. If I may move on, your Honours, to the next document, this document, the one I want to now go to, is 135, please. Your Honours, this document is also a membership-type, identity card-type document. It is in fact a membership card of the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action. Presumably it is the Vienna branch of that party or club, which may be a way of referring to it outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Your Honours, the document, in our submission, is relevant and admissible because it goes to issues of identity. It also interestingly -- it is also interesting from the point of view that it makes reference to the address. It gives the name "Zejnil Delalic", it gives his occupation as "translator" and in a document that I will refer to subsequently, there is a reference to the fact that when he initially went to Germany he worked as an interpreter in Germany, and that document, your Honour, I will not take you to it now, but it is Exhibit 144. We will come to that. Your Honours, the address that is shown there is, "1160 Vienna, Koppstrasse 16". Your Honours will recall that 1160 Vienna Koppstrasse is an address related to the premises INDA-BAU, where the search warrant was executed. Your Honours, this document, a copy of this document was also shown to the accused Mr. Delalic in the course of the record of interview that was had with him on 22nd and 23rd August 1996, and in relation to that, the investigator said to the accused

utterances.speaker: MR. DELALIC
utterances.text: "So in 1992, were you a member of any political party? Answer: No. Question: I am now showing you a copy of another document which was found during the search in Vienna on 18th March this year. There is a copy of a membership card of the SDA, dated 4th May 1992." This document here that I am now referring your Honours to, Exhibit 135. When the document was presented to the accused, Mr. Delalic said: "This is an Austrian, this is an Austrian and this is not a political party, this is like an association. Abroad, we are not entitled to set up political parties. This is just a club and somebody must have enrolled me into their membership. This is a cultural association which is active in Austria. Question: Did you pay anything to this party? Answer: When you said 'pay', you mean membership fees? Question: Contribute fee, or in another way contribute money to the party? Answer: Yes", and I think this is coming from the interpreter, "he said he thinks he gave them some money and he gave them money for humanitarian purposes." There are a number of questions that go back and forth in relation to this document and finally the accused said: "I have no reason to hide this from you because this was a legal party, but what I have to say is that in Austria we are not entitled to set up a political party, it is just an association, a club. We have no political background and I was a member of that club, SDA club, in Austria. I am not a member of the SDA in Konjic. This club is very pro SDA and as far as I can remember, political parties in 1992 in Konjic, they were not even operational, none of them, not to talk about the SDA." Nothing in that, your Honours, to suggest that this was a document that somebody had mischievously forged and placed in the premises of INDA-BAU so as to mislead your Honours that this forgery indicated anything other than what it says. In my submission, your Honours, clearly it is an authentic document; it is a document that was found among the other papers in the premises and when shown to Officer Moerbauer during the course of his testimony, he said, at page 3564, lines 18 to 22: "This ID card was in binder I7, and was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, in the Vienna police headquarters." Your Honours, it is in our submission an authentic document, as are the other documents that we have referred you to in the course of this submission. The next document, your Honours, if I may move on, is document 137, if it may for a moment be displayed. This document has been admitted into evidence through General Pasalic when he testified here. It is the document that relates to the arrest warrants of the people therein mentioned, and a request for an Interpol warrant to be issued against the accused Delalic and Mucic. As I say, it has been admitted into evidence, but it was acknowledged as a document of General Pasalic. There was no suggestion by him in any way that it was a forgery or a fake, or that anyone had maliciously created it or otherwise. It was a document he immediately recognised and your Honours accepted it into evidence. Moving on, your Honours, to document 141, if I may have the first page of that document displayed on the screen. I have referred your Honours to Exhibit 141 on a number of occasions. This document has been accepted, it has been admitted into evidence and accepted as an authentic document. It was authenticated by General Pasalic in the course of his testimony. It relates to those charges. It is a document which describes the accused Delalic as commander of the first Tactical Group and a high ranking officer in the army of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with, "great and wider responsibility". It describes him in that fashion. He was asked various questions about that, this document, and following questioning in relation to the document, that is General Pasalic was asked questions about it, it was tendered and accepted into evidence. Your Honours, if I may go to the next document, document 143. This document is in typewritten form. It is not signed and it does bear the date 7th December, with a heading, "Mostar, 7th December". It appears to be presented in the format that one occasionally sees the drafts of press releases, but it may not be that. It is simply a typewritten document that was found among other documents there. This document, your Honours, as I say, commences at the very top of the page . "Mostar, 7th December". Then it says: "The commander of the BH-Army. The 4th Corps, Arif Pasalic, has informed today's press conference that 22 BH-Army members have been arrested on reasonable grounds for suspecting that they have been engaged", and then he proceeds to set out the allegations. Your Honours know from Exhibit 137 and from an array of other documents that this in fact happened, that allegations and arrests were made by Arif Pasalic, then commander of the 4th Corps, and that was an event that is well known. In the second paragraph, it goes on to say: "Commander Pasalic stated that the assistant commander of the first Tactical Group, Edib Saric", and your Honours, I have taken you to a number of documents dealing with Edib Saric as the assistant commander of the accused Zejnil Delalic. This is again a reference to him. It says, "has also been arrested", and your Honours will recall that in that list of names in Exhibit 137, the list of names of persons to be detained, the name of Edib Saric appears. He is again referred to as assistant: "The names of the other arrested persons have been kept secret for the time being. The key figure of the affair, Zejnil Delalic, commander of the first Tactical Group, has escaped." It again refers to him in that position, referring to him as "escaped"; it is well known from numerous other documents that I have shown your Honours in the course of this submission that he left on 25th November at 8.00 pm. It then goes on: "It has been reported that he used his connection with Serbian troops whose helicopter took him from the area of Kobiljaca to Belgrade and then to Vienna, where he owns a private firm." Your Honours will recall how vociferously the accused Delalic, in numerous documents that have been presented to you in the course of this submission, has spoken of how the Croatian media made up this story about the helicopter escape. I know this is Mostar, but presumably it was not limited only to Croatia where that occurred. It goes on and says: "The commander of the Celebici prison, Zdravko Mucic, also called Pavo, managed to escape with him." Then it goes on and sets out those details. At the bottom of the page it says: "Commander Pasalic has confirmed that General Jovan Divjak, also a member of BH-Army staff, is also detained in Konjic." The first page of this document, your Honours, goes to that question of its consistency with other documents I have shown you. It has its relevance in the sense that it refers to the position held by the accused Delalic and the accused Mucic, but its significance, in my submission, is it confirms that thread of evidence that appears to run through all of these documents in relation to these events and so is primarily significant for that purpose. This document, again, when shown to the witness Moerbauer, he said: "This document was in binder I10, and was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at Vienna police headquarters." He says this at page 3654, lines 4 to 7 of the transcript. If we could move on now, your Honours, to the next document, 144, this document was located at the premises of INDA-BAU. It is a typewritten document, it is an extensive document. At the end of the document there is hand-written: "Geneva, 14th December 1992, Zejnil Delalic", and then the abbreviation of commander of Tactical Group 1. This, your Honour, appears to be also a document in the form of some sort of report. It seems to be a report, again it is an extensive report, on the incidents that occurred in Konjic during the period 1992, when the accused Delalic was there, and provides an explanation for the accused's role in those events, to the course of that period of time again your Honours, as I said, this document was found at the premises of INDA-BAU, and when presented to Officer Moerbauer, at page 3656, lines 8 to 10, Officer Moerbauer said: "This document was in a binder I/11 and was handed to me by my colleague, Navrat, at Vienna police headquarters." The document speaks of the command authority in Konjic of the accused Delalic and his authority over people in the municipalities. It starts off, if your Honours please, with a reference to those Croatian newspapers that we have heard so much about in the course of this submission, where it says in the first paragraph at the top of the page: "Almost all Croatian newspapers, some even in instalments, have recently published downright lies about my escape from Konjic to Belgrade and further afield." In my submission, your Honour, again consistent with what we have already heard in relation to that. In the next paragraph, the second sentence: "Had not my Chetnik-made helicopter, chopper, or whatever you want to call it, broken down, I would have flown all over Europe. But an end to jokes, because this might cost me or someone else his life." Your Honours, the document then goes on to say in the next paragraph and in the third sentence, in about the middle of the next paragraph, starting: "I was in charge as a commander of the Tactical Group for all inconvenience and maltreatment they have suffered because of me." This document, your Honours, also give biographical background to the accused which is also referred to in a number of the documents that we have referred to in the course of this submission. I will come to that at the very bottom of the last paragraph here. It says in the last paragraph on the first page, second sentence: "One of such things is my connection with KOS, or whatever it is called. This is absolutely true. Our connections goes back to 1968 when I was a student at the arts faculty in Sarajevo." Then it speaks of demonstrations that took place at that stage and his role as a student. Then turning over the page on to page 2, the first very long paragraph, six lines from the top of the page: "At the end of 1970, I left for Germany to work as an interpreter. I still have my business connections with Germany and some other neighbouring countries." Your Honours will recall from the identity card that we examined a moment ago the reference to his role, there described as a translator, here described as an interpreter. Going over to the next page, page 3, under the heading, "Arms and ammunition smuggling", which your Honours may recall was one of the allegations that had been raised at some stage, your Honours, in the second paragraph under that heading, there he speaks of coming to Konjic in March: "I brought as much money as I had at the time. I and a few friends organised the Muslim population and got in touch with the already existing HVO, who were operating underground. We worked day and night until June. We had great results." He speaks then of the distribution of weapons. The next paragraph down, starting: "I bought 2,000 uniforms", and your Honours will recall references to these uniforms in other documents that we have seen in the course of this submission. Exhibit 124 was an example of that. Then he speaks of buying the equipment, fuel et cetera, "with my own money". Then he distributed it according to needs. Four lines down, he then makes reference to the reward of 10,000 German Marks: "... to anyone who can confirm or testify that I sold him a single bullet, radio transmitter, et cetera." Your Honours will recall in other exhibits we looked at, Exhibits 117 and 124 in particular, there is a reference to this offer of reward to anyone who could come forward and prove that allegation. Then in the next paragraph, there is a reference to the end of June: "Our HVO formed a completely separate command." Again, a completely consistent theme we have seen in numerous of the other documents that we have referred to. Again it says: "At the beginning of July, I was in charge of an operation which was the first attempt at liberating Borci. The HVO did not take part in that operation." Again that is consistent with what we have seen in other documents. Over the page on page 4, in the first main paragraph, we see a reference there to the fact that he was appointed to commander of Tactical Group 1. Then in the centre of that paragraph, there is a reference to Edib Saric: "In addition, the three commanders of the lines of attack were temporarily appointed only for that operation. Edib Saric was in charge of the right line." Then if we can move down to the next paragraph, it reads: "I was in Konjic until the end of June. I took part in actions, including the seizure of the Celebici barracks. This was the first barracks to be taken in Bosnia-Herzegovina." He speaks of being leader of about 20 volunteers when he took that barracks. Then he makes reference towards the bottom of the page to Esad Ramic: "... who, after I was appointed commander of TG1, paraded for two months, taking oaths and forming a brigade which was never formed, and boycotting all orders by the TG1 and supreme command. I would like to emphasise that the consequences of such behaviour were unimaginable." In our submission, your Honour, that is a very relevant aspect of this document when speaking of the structure that was operating there and who was giving orders to who. Over the page, at page 5 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the passage you were just reading, there was one very interesting sentence. He says: "From August, I had no connections at all with the headquarters", although according to the evidence he was appointed as commander of all formations. I was just reading that: "From August on, I had no connection with the Konjic headquarters apart from passing on the orders of the supreme command"; just acting as a post office, although according to you, he was the commander of all formations in Konjic. I am reading from, "from August on".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, your Honour. From August 1992, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was appointed as commander of all forces I think 8th August or 9th August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All formations, commander of Tactical Group in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tactical Group 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 11th or 12th July, and then he was appointed as commander of all formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do believe there is another document, it is not part of these documents, but I do believe we have seen another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are relying on this document, if you have to take the document as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of course, your Honour. I do not have that other one to hand. Your Honour, we do not deny that there may be different interpretations placed on different things. Like all things, there is good and bad for the Prosecution in these documents. We are aware of that. Whether this is bad for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just wondering, because despite his being appointed as commander of all formations, the Konjic municipality still retained its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I noticed that, your Honour. It does go on to say, in the sense that there is ambiguity, in relation to the role of Ramic, he speaks of how he was appointed TG1 parader for two months. After he was appointed, Ramic, "paraded for two months, taking oaths and forming brigades which were never formed, and boycotting" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was just looking at this letter, I just read that sentence and thought I would draw your attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving on, your Honours, at page 5, in the centre of the page, again there is a reference to Colonel Divjak, and how ultimately he comes to Konjic when the accused is there at that time. Over on the next page, page 6, in the very centre of the page, there is a paragraph: "It is interesting that from March 1992 right up until 25th November 1992, 2000 hours", that time 8.00 at night again, "I was constantly in the area of my responsibility without taking a day off, going anywhere or doing anything else. I was available 24 hours a day, except for a trip to Zagreb at the beginning of March, where I was sent against my will at the request of the supreme command".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: March or May?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It says "March" here. It says "March" on this copy. Then over the page on page 7, there is a reference to, "Escape in Chetnik helicopter", a heading there and then in the second paragraph, third from the bottom, it says: "I left a report in handwriting", et cetera. The last sentence of that paragraph: "The Croatian side checked my passport in the computer and the Austrians stamped the date of my crossing, 26th November 1992, as Spielfeld. As we all know, helicopters do not land in Spielfeld, particularly Chetnik ones." Then over on page 8, towards the bottom of the page, just before the commencement of the very last paragraph, the last sentence of the very long paragraph, it says: "Saric, who replaced me until TG1 was completely disbanded, was previously at Mt. Igman with a completely different group which was later also disbanded due to the reorganisation of the brigade." Then finally, your Honour, going to page 10 of the document, the very last page of the document, the very last sentence: "The intention of Zejnil Delalic, Edib Saric and several others was not to prevent this at all, but to solely fight Chetniks." Then it is signed, "Zejnil Delalic, Commander of Tactical Group 1, Geneva, 14th December 1992". Your Honours, this is a very long document. It does deal with the accused directly in a biographical sense. It deals with him in his role in Konjic; it deals with his involvement with the army there, with the establishment of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in its early days, its infancy and how he contributed to it; it deals with his role in the seizure of the Celebici barracks and his role as Tactical Group 1 commander. In my submission, your Honours, it is a document that bears a considerable degree of indicia of reliability and should as a consequence be admitted into evidence. The next document, your Honours, is Exhibit 145, if that could be shown on the screen. Your Honour, this Exhibit 145 is also a document that was found in the premises of INDA-BAU, and was referred to by me earlier only for one purpose and one purpose alone, and that is it appears to contain a reference to Article 217 of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, which was adopted as the law of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In our submission the only relevance of it is that it goes to that point and tends to support the other documents where these charges were made. It also goes with those class of documents which deal with the collection of material that was found, the collection of material which, when assembled, represents a rebuttal, as it were, of the allegations that were made against the accused. In that sense, in our submission, it is relevant for that purpose only, and is admissible. Your Honours, moving on then to the next document, this document, 146, if that could be displayed on the screen, this is a document, your Honours, that is also in a hand-written form. Again, it was found on the premises of INDA-BAU. This document was shown to the witness Moerbauer. He said of it, at page 3656, line 14 to 16: "This was in binder I/11 and was also handed to me by my colleague, Navrat." As I say, it is headed, "Hazim", it does not bear a date, nor does it bear a signature. It does appear to relate to those incidents which are referred to in the allegations raised by General Pasalic when charges were made. The Prosecution seek to rely on it only for its reference to the structure of the chain of command which was referred to in the centre page, the centre paragraph of the document, which says: "I never received any orders or instructions from Commander Delalic. There were at least two immediate levels in the chain of command, prison commander of the municipal headquarters, and then TG1 commander." If this document was written by the deputy of the prison commander, Mucic, then one would understand, in my submission, the description of the chain of command that is being referred to there. That is the only aspect of this particular document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who has written this note? Who is the author of this note?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does not say, your Honour, but I refer to the top of the page where it says "Note - Hazim".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Who is the author? One does not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, one does not know who wrote it, but it may be a version of events described by the accused Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: When was it written?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It would appear to have been written after the charges or proceedings had been commenced by General Pasalic at the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So there is no one who can own the authorship of this note?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You rely upon this document to show the command structure, is it not a little far-fetched?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On its own, your Honours, I would admit to the fact that there may well be difficulty in doing that, if that was all we had to present to you; but if we present it to you consistent with a whole raft of other documents which do the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So the relevancy of a note whose authorship is not known --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours, it was something found at the premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It may be found at the premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Presumably if it was inconsistent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You rely upon that, something which is consistent, when deciding the question of relevancy? It is a note, one does not know who wrote it, when it was written, in what connection it was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may be all these documents in handwriting were written by the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Obviously it does not refer to Hazim Delic, or does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It obviously does, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is there anything in the note that suggests it refers to Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The name at the top, "Hazim".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Hazim is a very common Muslim name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: True, but not all Hazims were in a position to receive instructions from Commander Delalic. There were at least two levels of the chain of command, prison commander and commander of the municipal headquarters, and then TG1 commander. I would have only thought the evidence points to one person in that position, and that is the accused, Hazim Delic. Moerbauer, as I said, referred to this as being in binder I/11. We can now go to the next document, 147A, if that could be placed on the screen, please? This document is partly in handwriting and partly typed. It is a pro forma-type document with the particular details being filled in. Your Honours, it is a registration card of the United Association of War Veterans of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The registration card pertains to the person, first name "Delalic", second name "Zejnil". Your Honours, it relates to the accused Delalic. It gives the date of birth, place of birth, it then gives the address as before the war, and it says, "Austria, Vienna", and then the street and house name is, "Taubergasse 15". Your Honours have heard Taubergasse in Vienna, Austria in relation to the search warrants. Then there is an address given in Konjic. It sets out then the education, speaks of the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo, translation college 1972, international social law in Stuttgart in 1974. There is a reference then to the languages, German, English and so forth. The next relates to joining the resistance in March 1992: "Political organisation: War Presidency. Military organisation: Konjic OSTO (Territorial Defence Municipal Headquarters)." Then describes the unit as the Konjic OSTO command, at the very bottom: "Duty: Co-ordinator between the OS armed forces and the RP War Presidency, afterwards the commander of Tactical Group 1." It then refers to: "Decorations and criminal proceedings: none." It gives then family details on the second page and then goes on to political activities. He was a member of the League of Communists from 1968 to 1972, then membership in political parties: "Member of: SDA from its establishment to present." It goes on to say: "Functions in the party: member of the main board of the Austrian SDA, Vienna. Member of: SDA." In our submission, your Honours, this is a document found on the premises, it is a document that when shown to Officer Moerbauer, at page 3656, lines 17 to 24, said: "These documents were located in binder I/11 and these documents, copies were made of these documents for the Tribunal on 18th March 1996. Of these documents, only copies of these documents were found in the police files." He said: "So for these documents, I made two copies, one for the people from the Tribunal and one for the police administration. A mistake must have been made in that the original must have been handed over to the people of the Tribunal as a copy".

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to ask, is my friend tendering a photocopy that was in a folder, or an original that somehow left the police headquarters that night? Which of the two is being tendered here? Here we are glossing all over the fact that on the night of the 18th March things were examined, photocopied and removed and taken away, so which is it? Is it the photocopy that was in a folder, or the card that disappeared from police headquarters that night?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I see the original?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know whether you want to argue it now or whether you prefer to challenge it by your own submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It was just unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Even if he did, until you have made your own submissions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to file the document which is found in the folder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will decide whether it is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There is a reference, your Honours, to the testimony of Mr. d'Hooge, where he speaks of receiving this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The one which is recovered from the premises?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will have that reference to the testimony located and take your Honours to it. Your Honours, if I could see the document that the Registrar has in her papers there, I might be able to answer the question now anyway. May I see the copy of Exhibit 147A? (Handed). It appears that it may be a copy by looking at it, your Honours, but it appears that it has been attached to something, so it is possible there was never an original, as such. I will have that matter investigated, your Honour. Your Honours, the next document, again found on the premises, 147B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which was the last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The registration card.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is B, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is B. This document is merely tendered because it relates to, as it were, 147A, the two of them being connected, both relating to the War Veterans' Association. It has no other significance other than that. It was found on the premises, it is signed, "Z Delalic", it is in hand-written form, it is dated Vienna, 24th November 1994, and again they fall into the same category when shown to Officer Moerbauer. He said at page 3656 of the transcript, at lines 17 to 24: "These documents were located in binder I/11 and these documents, copies were made of these documents for the Tribunal on 18th March 1992 and these documents, only copies of these documents were found in the police files. So for those documents I made two copies, one for the people from the Tribunal and one for the police administration. A mistake must have been made and the original must have been handed over to the people of the Tribunal as a copy." Again, I believe this is a document referred to by Mr. d'Hooge in his evidence. We can go to that in the course -- refer your Honours to that if necessary. The final document in the series of documents that we seek to tender is again a related document, Exhibit 147C, and if that please can be placed on the screen. Your Honours, this document is relied on by the Prosecution in a similar way to the previous document, this time in relation to the identity card of the Green Berets, which was referred to previously in my submission as a document which was shown to the accused in the course of his interview by officers of the Tribunal, on 26th August 1996, and relates to in the same way Exhibit 133, the Green Berets card. He makes reference to the fact in the letter that the Green Berets had been established in Konjic, that it was working. It then describes the members of those who first started the resistance: "... who have not forgotten the truth and whose aims and tasks were to get to the facts, memories and proof about the establishment of operations. The founding assembly was held on November 1994." It is consistent with what he had said in his record of interview. Again, your Honours, this letter was shown to Officer Moerbauer, it fell into the same category as documents that were located in binder I/11, and copies were made of the document for the Tribunal on 18th March 1996, and he goes on to say for those documents he made two copies, one for the people from the Tribunal and one for police administration. He says a mistake must have been made in that the original must have been handed over to the people at the Tribunal, instead of the copy being handed over. We submit, your Honours, that having regard to where it was found, to what it relates, that it is a document that fits into that pattern of evidence that is properly admissible and has the relevant indicia of authenticity. Those then, your Honours, are our submissions in relation to the documents themselves. The next issue that it is necessary for us to address is the videotapes that were also seized from the premises of INDA-BAU, and in addition to the videotapes at INDA-BAU, the videotapes that were recovered from the premises of the accused Mucic when Officer Panzer went to the premises of Mr. Mucic and executed the search warrant, and was then -- and then did recover certain videotapes, some of which have been played in the course of the evidence. For example, the first videotape to be played and admitted into evidence is the videotape that contains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you start on the videotapes, let us get our bearing right, because the evidence which was led here did not reveal that there was an accurate count of the videotapes as was recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: An accurate count, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, of the videotapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There was reference to that in relation to the INDA-BAU tapes, but not all the tapes came from INDA-BAU. A group of the tapes, ones that we will deal with first, came from the premises of the accused Mucic. The testimony of Mr. Panzer is that when he went there with the search warrant to recover those premises, he said that he asked Mr. Mucic whether he had any videotapes relevant to the Celebici camp -- in fact, I have been handed part of the transcript here. These videotapes from the premises of Mr. Mucic were recovered by Officer Panzer in the following way; at page 6444, line 11, Officer Panzer said, in relation to the videotapes recovered from the premises of Mr. Mucic: "I talked to Mr. Mucic and I told him we were looking for documents relevant to war crimes in Bosnia; in particular, there were to be videotapes of Celebici camp that he had made, and he said he did not have anything of that sort, but there were videos with footage from the Celebici camp. I asked him, 'where are those videotapes?' Thereupon, we entered the living room and there is a piece of furniture there up against the wall. He took out some tapes, a dozen or so. He put those tapes on the table and then he picked out from the pile four videotapes and in respect of these, he said there were the reports about the war, footage of destruction and footage of all, shall we say, entertainment activities at the camp." So your Honours, in relation to the videotapes recovered from the premises of Mr. Mucic, there is no issue at all about numbering or anything of the sort. It was straightforward, they were given to him by Mr. Mucic, they were given in the context when Officer Panzer was searching for relevant information, relevant videotapes, they were handed to him by the accused Mucic in response to the request by the officer. In my submission, your Honours, there could be no more authentic way, no more reliable way for information to come to this court than by such process where the accused himself presents the material to the officer conducting the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You started with a general discussion of videotapes. Where there is a mix-up as to whether the number of videotapes recovered varied in terms of numbers as recorded, you have to separate those which there is no dispute as to the numbers from those to which there are disputes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, and I have done that, your Honours, in terms of referring to the Mucic tapes. They are to be distinguished from the INDA-BAU tapes where there is dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Not now, I did not hear that. You just opened your statement with the question of tapes. You just opened your address with the question of videotapes, and this is why I tried to narrow it down as to those with which there are difficulties in determining the number which were recovered and those in which there is no difficulty. This is what I wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. There is no difficulty with the Mucic tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, so by the time you make your arguments, we will understand which you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On the Mucic tapes, there are no disputes, only the INDA-BAU tapes. The Mucic tapes; there may well be dispute about their admissibility, I would be surprised if there was not, but it is not a result of there being a mix-up of numbers. Your Honours, I have prepared a list of the -- I have prepared extracts of each of these videotapes. It seems to me that the easiest way to deal with it is to deal with the transcript of the tape itself as a way of illustrating the relevance of the words, of the spoken word that appears on the tape. We can go back and play the tape, if that would assist your Honours, but it seems to me that just for the purposes of dealing with admissibility, it is probably better to first deal with the transcript. I am not tendering the transcript as evidence as such, but I am using it as an aide memoire to assist in the discussion about its relevance. Then we can view the video with the aide memoire, if your Honours wish to follow that course, because it is, of course, the videotapes themselves, that is the evidence we seek to tender, and not the transcripts of the words that appear on it which has been translated into the English language. I have a copy for -- one each for counsel for the Defence and one each for your Honours. If that could be handed up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Perhaps these videotapes have already been played in the court. One was a birthday party, the other was one of the witnesses being asked to do some exercises. I forget, but I remember two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have ideas of particular scenes contained in the videotapes which you want to play back. Even if they have already been played, I suppose you might mention it, we will take it into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will do that, your Honour, and mention the ones that have been played. The first videotape, Exhibit 109, that has been admitted already. It is an exhibit, so it has been admitted into evidence. It has also been played to your Honours, so the first one we deal with is Exhibit 110. Would your Honour excuse me a minute? (Pause). My understanding, your Honours, is that the whole of Exhibit 109 is admitted and accepted in evidence. I do not know if there is any dispute about that, but that is how I understand the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The person who prepared those videos, the driver, has already been examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is also a video that had been played by the Defence as well, it is a short video I understand. But in any event, I will come back to it if necessary, but my understanding is that it is admitted. Exhibit 110 then is the first video that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will have the short break now. We will come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, can we hear you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms McMurrey, for unavoidable reasons, is unable to be with us for the rest of the afternoon. I also want to bring the court up to date on the latest Landzo report. That is that arrangements have been made for him to see the doctor, apparently around noon tomorrow. The request is that we adjourn at 11.30 and remain in adjournment until 2.30. They can take him to see the doctor and have him back here in time for the 2.30 session. That would be my request and I think it is a reasonable one and appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber thought it might be unfair for him not to see the doctor tomorrow, since there was no specific appointment for him for the Friday, which we thought, so we are very pleased. It is better he sees his doctor at that time, but if he still needs special treatment, then the appointment can be made for him to see the doctor some other time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I want to again express my appreciation and that of my client for your and the other judges' sensitivity to his situation. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I was asking you before the break, have not these tapes been proved by the person who took them? I will not name him, the driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is why I will not name him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One of the tapes was, your Honour, by the driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I probably mentioned two or three tapes. One was about the birthday party, one was taking exercises, one of the detainees, who is also a protected witness, and then certain scenes from the streets of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That was the first one, I think, your Honour. The streets of Konjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They were all in one tape then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I think they are different tapes, your Honour. The streets of Konjic I think is the first tape, 109. If I may just check for a moment? It is a funeral scene, starts off with a funeral scene. I think that one has been admitted. There is also the one that your Honour speaks of, where the driver attested to taking part of it. Not all of that went into evidence, but only part of it, the part that he says he was involved in taking it. There is another tape, which was a tape of an interview given by the witness Pasalic, and it has been tendered too. That is Exhibit 114.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Which still leaves some tapes unproved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, it does. The Pasalic tape was the INDA-BAU tape. There are some which have not been done yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I was just suggesting, of course you can tender everything which is legally permissible, I was just mentioning that we had some tapes recovered from Mucic's apartment allegedly identified by him to persons carrying out the search. Of course you know your case better. I will not stop you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which are we now concentrating on?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The first one is Exhibit 110. Your Honours have been handed a transcript, I think. It is easier, I think, to deal with a transcript. It should have at the top of the page "MIB".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which of the segments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Segment 1. Your Honours, I must say at the outset that without the tape playing, it loses, just relying on the transcript, it loses some of its relevance, so if there is some -- if your Honours are concerned about the relevance of a certain aspect of the tape, it is our submission that that relevance is enhanced by a viewing of the actual material itself, and certainly the best way to do it is to see it, but I am trying to do it as efficiently and quickly as possible. I think I can do it by submission, just relying on the written material, but if I am unsuccessful on that, I will have to revert to actually showing it, which I will try to avoid for the moment. There will be some stage, presumably before the end of the case, when the parts that we wish to emphasise, in submission or otherwise, will be played at that stage, but if I can proceed on this basis at the moment, we can see whether or not it can be established. Your Honours, the Exhibit 110, referred to as "MIB", this document, as I said, was recovered from the premises of Mr. Mucic. It was shown to Officer Moerbauer at page 3622 of the transcript, line 22. Officer Moerbauer said: "Here again, MIB, both the tape and the case, and therefore stem from the apartment of Mucic." At page 6505, line 24 and 6506, line 1, the tape was shown to Officer Panzer, and he said: "I can remember this tape as well for two reasons: first of all because of the word written here 'Celebici', that is written on there, and then secondly because of the sticker MIB. I wrote that on here and I put the sticker on the tape and then on the case has the same sticker, 'M' for Mucic, 'I' for the tape and 'B' because it is the second tape that we seized." Then at page 6506, lines 14 to 15, Panzer said: "This is also a tape that was handed to me by Mr. Mucic." Your Honours, the first segment, these are very short segments, and as I say, one only picks up part of the relevance of them from the words, but primarily, the reference by the accused Mucic to: "Zejnil said I must have had an arrangement with them." It then flows on at segment 2, arrives at the gate to the Celebici camp, the car that is being travelled in by the accused Mucic. There is a short segment there where the accused is photographing a soldier, who is saying "not me, please". We then go on to segment 3, which is referred to in that transcript, and it shows the administration building, building number 22, and briefly, inside the administration, there are some guards and the accused Delic. We submit that all of this is relevant as it goes to the camp itself, it goes to the authority of the accused Mucic who was driving in there. The reference to Zejnil --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The reference to Zejnil is not very clear, in what connection the statement attributed to Zejnil was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is true. It is as it appears there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The relevance is over Mucic's concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I acknowledge that, your Honour. Then the administration building and building number 22, which your Honours have heard so much reference to. Then there is reference to the army in segment 4: "Smajo, the army is grateful to you for the land you contributed down there." It is just a small point, but it is a reference to somebody in authority expressing their appreciation for the provision of food in the form of land to the army. Then in segment 5, it is a totally different segment then, this bears the date 16th August -- I am sorry. It is segment number 5, 01:19:15. There is a voice: "I would like to give the floor to the President of the War Presidency of our municipality, Dr Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic." Your Honours have seen reference to this gentleman on numerous occasions. Then he addresses the soldiers that are gathered there, congratulates them and speaks of laying the foundation for the forming of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Konjic area: "This is a historic moment, when all of us who have defended our country from the first days of the aggression", et cetera et cetera, and so a speech is given. Then an officer is seen on the video and he says: "I would like now to give the floor to the commander of Tactical Group 1 for lifting the blockade of Sarajevo, Mr. Zejnil Delalic." Then the accused Delalic addresses the soldiers. He speaks of greeting them and the units for Konjic, holding their positions, have demonstrated they are ready for combat, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me just a minute. Just a suggestion, I think it is quite helpful that Mr. Niemann has provided us all with this aide memoire as he calls it; it seems to me it would be both merciful and efficient for him to simply point out what it is about these segments that he thinks make them relevant, rather than reading to us what we can all read a great deal faster than he can read it to us. We are all staying quite a way ahead of him and maybe it would be efficient for him to say, "I think this segment is relevant for this reason". Maybe we can move through this a lot faster, that is my hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It might be more helpful if you just point out the areas you emphasise. There are quite a number of segments and not all of them are relevant to what you want to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we say that segment 6 is relevant because it relates to the authority of the accused Mucic in relation to the camp. We have here the reference to a woman who wants to see a gentleman inside the camp, and is asking for permission to do that. There is a group of women gathered there who are endeavouring to do that. At first, the accused Mucic says that nobody can visit, it is a prison, that if he makes one exception then he has to make others. Ultimately he relents and grants permission for the woman to actually go in. So in our submission, your Honour, this clearly shows his authority in relation to the camp, shows his authority to allow people to make visits from time to time and his authority to refuse visits if that is requested. The next segment, segment 7 is a lengthy segment. It relates to a prisoner who was in the camp, a gentleman by the name of Hristo Zuza. Your Honours, there is evidence by a protected witness that it was generally considered that this gentleman was a person who was either mentally retarded or of very low mental ability. The segment that follows is a very lengthy -- there is a whole large segment that is produced then that follows, which we say goes to the issue of the treatment of these people when they are in the camp. There is nothing suggested that it is physical mistreatment at all, but having regard to the fact that this gentleman was mentally handicapped, that he was in the camp as a prisoner and he was Serbian, and then the way the accused Mucic then proceeds to treat him in those circumstances, in our submission, goes to the question of inhumane treatment. One has to see this in sequence, one has to read what was said, but on doing that, in our submission, we submit that this is evidence of inhumane treatment. Examples that appear, as the reference to: "Tell me, are you sleepy? Why are you blinking your eyes? "Prisoner: I was born like this." Then there is a voice that says in front of the accused Mucic: "Tell us, who is the greatest? "Prisoner: Allah. "Voice: Who? "Prisoner: Allah. "Voice: Who? "Prisoner: Allah, Allah, Allah." Then the accused Mucic asks how tall Allah is, and so forth. There are those references there and later on, the accused Mucic makes him recite things. Firstly he tells him to recite names of domestic animals and it is necessary for him to then recite, "horse, cow, sheep, lizard", et cetera, then further names of birds and he makes him recite those, then towns and then the prisoner is made to do that. It may on its face seem innocuous to us sitting here, but in those conditions, we would argue that having regard to his condition and what he was made to do, that this is evidence of that. Then it goes on, this is again a very long segment which gains its significance from seeing it as well as just reading it, but there is a reference there to a part there where Eda says: "Say: Sieg heil! "Prisoner: Sieg heil, sieg heil, sieg heil!" Then they talk about an incident which involves Hristo again and he is subjected to further, in our submission, inhumane treatment and ridicule at a time when he is dressed, he is dressed as a woman, and the accused Mucic says: "Wait a minute, you are not Tarzan, you are a woman now. "Voice: More gentle, more gentle." Then there is a whole lot of questions back and forth as this person was presented in this capacity as a woman, dressed as a woman. Then again there is this requirement for him to recite animals and fish and wild animals and so forth and this man is made to recite them, and he says: "Roe, sheep", and so forth, "kangaroo, salamander, squirrel", and there is references to that in the transcript. In our submission, all of this goes to that question of inhumane treatment of this man that was held in custody in the camp. Then there is segment 11, which in our submission shows the hangar number 6 and the machine-gun bunker. There is a question: "What is the situation there like? "Prisoner: Excellent. Mucic: What do you have to complain about, you are quite well off compared to what you guys would have done to us if you could." Then finally in segment 12, we have the gun being fired into the air and the prisoner ordered to do the push-ups which your Honour has referred to. Bearing in mind that the prisoner doing the push-ups is an elderly gentleman, he testified as to the difficulties that he had in having to do that. Finally there is the end scene, the administration of -- in the administration building of the Celebici camp. So all of that, when put collectively together, in our submission it is relevant for a range of reasons, it is relevant in the sense that it shows the accused Delalic and he is dealing with troops at the camp, and his relationship to the President of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, we object, the name Delalic is not mentioned anywhere but my learned friend has mentioned that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In segment 5 it is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just one sentence relating to Delalic: "Arrangements to be made." That is why I asked Mr. Niemann. That is a very vague sort of a reference to Delalic. What arrangements, with reference to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours, segment 5 over the page. Your Honour is referring to segment 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, that was the celebration of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The lifting of the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is the second page, segment 5 on the second page. So for what it shows, who it shows, for what it deals with, for the conversations that take place and those matters that I referred to, your Honours, having regard to the fact that it was a videotape actually handed to the officer, it is admissible, and we, along with everything else, move for its admission into evidence. I can move on to the next document, which is MIC, which is Exhibit 111. I will hand that up, your Honours. I understand your Honours do not have a copy of it. (Handed). Your Honours, this segment 1 of this tape relates to the unloading or the carrying of goods which appear to have been received. There is no explanation from the video as to where they came from or who provided them, but it would seem to be the receiving of supplies, and there is some discussion there of what is contained. At the top of the page, the soldier says: "Sure, film me, and then show it to the Chetniks up there."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED SAYS
utterances.text: "Zoka, that is him. Sieg heil! Let them film us together. This one too, son. We will get a lot of money from Milosevic for this tape. "Soldier: Let us get down to business." There then seems to be a counting off of material, "boots, 40 pairs, a case of ammunition for snipers", and so forth, it appears to relate to that. The reference further down is a reference to the fact that everybody wants to steal it and the accused Mucic says: "I am surprised about that. I thought that all thieves were in prison. You can send them to me. There is enough room for 2,000 more." In my submission, your Honours, that is a reference to the Celebici camp; "send them to me, there is room for 2,000 more" is a reference to the capacity to take more prisoners there. A man says: "Really? "Mucic: Just send them. I have dug a large hole there. "Man: When the Red Cross comes, let them see only the fresh ones. "Mucic: They may stay there if they dig too deep. "Man: Imagine that, a Red Cross mission arrested." Your Honours, clearly the issue of the Red Cross visiting and coming to the camp on occasions when they did was an issue of concern not only for the accused Mucic but the accused Delalic, and it was an issue that they were concerned about. Then over the page in segment 2: "'How can you let the Chetniks load that stuff?'" In our submission, your Honours, there is evidence of equipment, military equipment arriving at the Celebici camp, and we have evidence of witnesses who were assigned the duty to load this equipment or unload this equipment and pack it away. We have heard evidence of that in the course of the hearing. In our submission, the reference: "'How can you let Chetniks load that stuff?'", and the accused Mucic answers that, he asks a question of himself and then gives the answer: "They can take my gun, and if they have balls enough, they can shoot me, but they are afraid. Only, you must not give it to somebody who does not have a family", and the rest is inaudible. It is a short segment, Exhibit 111. This exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a brief remark; I made an error a moment ago, but now I have been following very carefully. Not in a single segment is the name of Mr. Delalic mentioned, but I understood that my learned colleague, because he is not mentioned, referred to him by saying that that was something worrying Mr. Delalic. I think it is necessary to present a document by its contents and not to make any allusions in connection with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are not trying to be fair with the procedure we have adopted. You will have your chance to reply and point out these things. I do not see any need why you should bother at this stage. Kindly continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. Your Honours, when this Exhibit 111 was shown to Mr. Panzer in the course of his evidence at page 6506, lines 17 to 20, he said: "This tape is one I remember, not on account of the label but rather on account of the sticker I put on here, 'MIC'. Once again, 'M' for Mucic, 'I' because it is a tape, and 'C' because it was the third tape I put a sticker on. The same reference on the case of the tape, and this is also a tape that was handed to me by Mr. Mucic and one that I had a brief look at in his apartment in his VCR." Your Honours, having regard to the contents of the tape, where it was taken, who it involved, who was seen in the tape and its relationship to the other evidence, the fact that it was given to Officer Panzer by the accused Mucic when the search warrant was executed on the premises I submit that properly it is relevant, it is properly admissible and should be admitted and I move its admission. Your Honour, excuse me. (Pause). Now if I could move on to the next exhibit, video Exhibit 112. This is referred to as "MID".

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that is being distributed, I just want to make sure in my own mind all the Prosecution is offering is what is in these excerpts, rather than the entire tape; am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
